title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
樊遲問仁子曰愛人問知子曰知人
文在中
同考試官教諭彭　批〔發明愛人知人精切渾融深得〕〔夫子語樊遲之意〕
考試官教諭張　批〔題本平易諸作騁浮議舊殊戾〕〔本旨此作詞簡義豊蓋邃于養者〕
考試官學正高　批〔明順精確模寫夫子語氣宛然〕
集士集士
===
聖人因賢者志於仁知而教以善用其心焉蓋
德愛曰仁通曰知人皆有是心也於此而知所
用焉仁知豈外是哉且道莫大於仁知夫固原
於一心而達之天下者也是故樊遲之在聖門
也以仁爲問焉夫子恐其近利之心易蔽以私
也乃告之曰仁主於愛而愛莫先於愛人其必
篤同類之誼而以恩相與務盡乎維持培植之
意擴民胞之度而以德相臨不失乎易直子諒
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

樊遲問仁，子曰：「愛人。」問知，子曰：「知人。」

文在中

同考試官教諭彭批〔發明愛人知人精切渾融，深得〕〔夫子語樊遲之意。〕

考試官教諭張批〔題本平易，諸作騁浮議，舊殊戾〕〔本旨。此作詞簡義豊，蓋邃于養者。〕

考試官學正高批〔明順精確，模寫夫子語氣宛然。〕

集士集士

聖人因賢者志於仁知，而教以善用其心焉。蓋德愛曰仁，通曰知，人皆有是心也。於此而知所用焉，仁知豈外是哉？且道莫大於仁知，夫固原於一心而達之天下者也。是故樊遲之在聖門也，以仁爲問焉。夫子恐其近利之心易蔽以私也，乃告之曰：「仁主於愛，而愛莫先於愛人。其必篤同類之誼，而以恩相與，務盡乎維持培植之意；擴民胞之度，而以德相臨，不失乎易直子諒
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Fan Chi asked about benevolence. The Master said, “Love others.” He asked about wisdom. The Master said, “Know others.”

Wen Zaizhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor: 〔The exposition of loving and knowing others is incisive, precise, and thoroughly integrated, deeply grasping〕〔the meaning of the Master's words to Fan Chi.〕

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔The topic is fundamentally straightforward. Other compositions indulge in superficial discussion, greatly departing [?] from〕〔its original meaning. This composition is concise in expression and rich in meaning; its author evidently possesses profound self-cultivation.〕

Comment by Examiner Gao, School Director: 〔Clear, fluent, precise, and exact: it vividly reproduces the Master's tone.〕

“Assemble scholars, assemble scholars” [?].

Because the worthy man aspired to benevolence and wisdom, the sage taught him to use his mind well. For, in virtue, love is called benevolence, and understanding is called wisdom; everyone possesses this mind. If one knows how to put it to use here, could benevolence and wisdom lie outside it? Moreover, nothing in the Way is greater than benevolence and wisdom: they indeed originate in the single mind and extend throughout the world. Thus, while Fan Chi was studying under the sage, he asked about benevolence. The Master feared that his inclination toward immediate advantage might easily be obscured by selfishness, and therefore told him: “Benevolence centers on love, and in love nothing takes precedence over loving others. One must strengthen the bonds that unite us with our own kind and treat others with kindness, striving to fulfill completely the intention of sustaining and nurturing them; one must broaden the disposition that regards the people as one's siblings and approach them with virtue, preserving ease, uprightness, childlike sincerity [?] …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
之東一體以爲心也四海以爲家也而分之恝
疎有不得而間之焉是雖仁統萬善若不盡於
愛人卽此而天下之至公在我所謂唯仁人能
愛人者此也不謂之仁而何哉又以智爲問焉
夫子慮其麤鄙之心易淆其真也乃告之曰智
主於知而知莫急於知人其必秉權度之精而
因言以考德務嚴夫淑慝之辨廣甄别之鑑而
緣迹以求心不爽乎是非之極以明覺則有常
也以品藻則不眩也而情之真僞有不能以逃
===
之焉是雖知周萬物若不盡於知人卽此而天
下之至明在我所謂惟知者不失人此也不謂
之知而何哉要之愛人仁也非知人則無以成
其愛知人知也非愛人則無以行其知夫子一
言而盡天下之道矣惜乎樊遲不足以語此抑
考書曰知人則哲能官人安民則惠黎民懷之
夫子此言固帝王治天下之要道也豈止爲樊
遲答問之敎哉雖然不有子夏富哉之論則夫
子枉直之敎將終晦矣昔人謂發聖人之蘊敎
punctuated: 之東。一體以爲心也，四海以爲家也，而分之恝疎，有不得而間之焉。是雖仁統萬善，若不盡於愛人，卽此而天下之至公在我，所謂「唯仁人能愛人」者，此也。不謂之仁而何哉？又以智爲問焉，夫子慮其麤鄙之心易淆其真也，乃告之曰：「智主於知，而知莫急於知人。」其必秉權度之精，而因言以考德，務嚴夫淑慝之辨；廣甄别之鑑，而緣迹以求心，不爽乎是非之極。以明覺則有常也，以品藻則不眩也，而情之真僞有不能以逃之焉。是雖知周萬物，若不盡於知人，卽此而天下之至明在我，所謂「惟知者不失人」，此也。不謂之知而何哉？要之，愛人，仁也；非知人，則無以成其愛。知人，知也；非愛人，則無以行其知。夫子一言而盡天下之道矣，惜乎樊遲不足以語此！抑考《書》曰：「知人則哲，能官人；安民則惠，黎民懷之。」夫子此言，固帝王治天下之要道也，豈止爲樊遲答問之敎哉？雖然，不有子夏「富哉」之論，則夫子枉直之敎將終晦矣。昔人謂發聖人之蘊，敎
translation_en:
…[The opening characters 之東 are doubtful: ?] One takes all people as a single body in one's heart and the four seas as one's family; callousness and estrangement arising from divisions cannot intrude. Although benevolence encompasses every goodness and seems not to be exhausted by loving others, it is precisely through this that the utmost impartiality under Heaven resides in oneself. This is what is meant by “Only the benevolent person can love others.” What could this be called but benevolence?

Fan Chi also asked about wisdom. Confucius, concerned that his coarse and uncultivated mind might readily obscure its true nature, told him: “Wisdom consists chiefly in knowing, and nothing is more urgent in knowing than knowing people.” One must hold to exact standards of judgment and assess virtue through people's words, taking care to distinguish strictly between goodness and wickedness. One must broaden one's discernment and seek people's hearts through their deeds, without departing from the ultimate standard of right and wrong. In lucid awareness one is constant; in appraising people one is not bewildered. Thus the sincerity or falseness of their dispositions cannot escape one's discernment. Although wisdom comprehends the myriad things and seems not to be exhausted by knowing people, it is precisely through this that the utmost discernment under Heaven resides in oneself. This is what is meant by “Only the wise do not misjudge people.” What could this be called but wisdom?

In essence, loving people is benevolence, but without knowing people one cannot bring that love to fulfillment. Knowing people is wisdom, but without loving people one cannot put that wisdom into practice. In a single utterance Confucius encompassed the Way of all under Heaven. How regrettable that Fan Chi was not equal to discussing this!

Moreover, consider what the Book of Documents says: “Knowing people constitutes discernment, enabling one to appoint them to office; bringing peace to the people constitutes kindness, and the common people cherish such a ruler.” These words of Confucius are indeed the essential Way by which emperors and kings govern all under Heaven. How could they be merely an instruction given in answer to Fan Chi's question? Nevertheless, without Zixia's observation, “How rich in meaning!”, Confucius's teaching about the crooked and the upright would have remained obscure forever. A man of former times spoke of bringing to light the sage's hidden meaning and teaching …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
萬世無窮者顏子也斯於子夏亦云
唯天下至聖爲能聰明睿知足以有臨也
邢鳳毛
同考試官教諭謝　批　〔聰明睿知一法發用即非生質此作〕
考試官教諭張　批　〔專主蘊蓄在心且下句以有臨取足於聰明睿知非造理精密曷有是作宜高薦〕
考試官學正高　批　〔體認精到發揮明徹〕
〔瑩潔純正足冠多士〕
聖人質超乎天下而君道豫焉蓋居上克明君
道也聖人獨稟乎生知之質有不足以居上而
===
臨下也哉中庸明天道意謂天地聖人相爲一
體者也觀天道之小德者亦觀之聖人而已矣
何則聖人者同賦于天而爲天之獨厚者也同
具于人而爲人之特出者也故自其質而言之
清淑之畀于太和者旣獨鍾夫純粹之正虛靈
之凝于保合者又克全其明覺之常內境昭融
而不睹不聞之中聰明具焉一天道之濬通而
無所蔽也神靈天啓而無思無爲之地睿知存
焉一日月之貞明而不可眩也夫然則萃繼明
punctuated:
萬世無窮者，顏子也。斯於子夏亦云。

唯天下至聖，爲能聰明睿知，足以有臨也。
邢鳳毛

同考試官教諭謝批〔聰明睿知一法發用即非生質此作〕
考試官教諭張批〔專主蘊蓄在心，且下句以有臨取足於聰明睿知，非造理精密，曷有是作？宜高薦。〕
考試官學正高批〔體認精到，發揮明徹。〕〔瑩潔純正，足冠多士。〕

聖人質超乎天下，而君道豫焉。蓋居上克明，君道也。聖人獨稟乎生知之質，有不足以居上而臨下也哉？中庸明天道，意謂天地、聖人相爲一體者也。觀天道之小德者，亦觀之聖人而已矣。何則？聖人者，同賦于天，而爲天之獨厚者也；同具于人，而爲人之特出者也。故自其質而言之，清淑之畀于太和者，旣獨鍾夫純粹之正；虛靈之凝于保合者，又克全其明覺之常。內境昭融，而不睹不聞之中，聰明具焉，一天道之濬通而無所蔽也；神靈天啓，而無思無爲之地，睿知存焉，一日月之貞明而不可眩也。夫然，則萃繼明
translation_en:
…for all ages without end: such was Master Yan. This may also be said of Zixia.

“Only the utmost sage under Heaven can possess the acuity of hearing and sight, sagacity, and wisdom sufficient to preside over others.”
Xing Fengmao

Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor, comments: 〔The passage concerning acuity, sagacity, and wisdom, their manifestation in activity, and their distinction from innate endowment is garbled [?].〕
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔The essay concentrates on what is stored within the mind. Moreover, in the latter clause, the capacity to preside over others derives its sufficiency from acuity, sagacity, and wisdom. Without a precise and penetrating grasp of principle, how could one produce such an essay? It merits recommendation at a high rank.〕
Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: 〔Its apprehension is precise and thorough; its exposition lucid and clear.〕〔Luminous, pure, and correct, it deserves to rank foremost among the many candidates.〕

The sage’s innate endowment surpasses that of all under Heaven, and the Way of the ruler is already contained within it. For to occupy a superior position and be capable of illumination is the Way of the ruler. The sage alone is endowed with the capacity to know from birth: could he lack what is sufficient to occupy the superior position and preside over those below? In elucidating the Way of Heaven, the Doctrine of the Mean means that Heaven, Earth, and the sage form a single body. To observe the lesser powers of the Way of Heaven, one need only observe the sage. Why is this? The sage receives his endowment from Heaven like everyone else, yet Heaven has treated him with singular generosity. He possesses what is common to humanity, yet stands out uniquely among human beings.

Thus, speaking of his innate endowment, the clear and excellent qualities bestowed through the Supreme Harmony are uniquely concentrated in him in their purest rectitude. The spiritual receptivity consolidated through the preservation of harmony also fully maintains its constant clarity of awareness. His inner realm is luminous and thoroughly integrated: amid what is neither seen nor heard, acuity of hearing and sight is fully present. It is wholly like the profound, unobstructed pervasiveness of the Way of Heaven. His spiritual intelligence is opened by Heaven: in the realm of neither thought nor action, sagacity and wisdom abide. It is wholly like the constant brightness of sun and moon, which cannot be obscured. This being so, he gathers successive illumination …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
于一心而所以照四方者取之淵微而自足會
明哲以作則而所以君萬邦者資之靜存而有
餘以之兼聽而聰足焉以之並觀而明足焉是
雖藏用而用之斯顯凡以理萬幾而宰羣動者
將無所事作而足乎已矣其諸天之光明下濟
而旁燭于無疆乎以之思微而睿足焉以之徧
物而知足焉是惟無感而感之斯通凡以式百
官而御萬民者將無事自用而有餘裕矣其諸
日月之重明麗天而照臨于無外乎夫生知之
===
質具而知臨之宜得如此由是四德之良皆從
此出而以容以執以敬以別莫非有臨之資矣
非天下之至聖其孰能與于斯哉雖然生知至
堯舜極矣書紀堯之欽明舜之濬哲而必繼之
允恭允塞蓋有誠敬之實而後生知可充也况
乎孔子告哀公以誠之之功而終之以雖愚必
明氣質之不足恃且拘也審矣故曰人主務聰
明之實
其爲氣也至大至剛以直養而無害則塞
punctuated:
于一心，而所以照四方者，取之淵微而自足；會明哲以作則，而所以君萬邦者，資之靜存而有餘。以之兼聽而聰足焉，以之並觀而明足焉。是雖藏用，而用之斯顯，凡以理萬幾而宰羣動者，將無所事作而足乎已矣。其諸天之光明下濟，而旁燭于無疆乎？以之思微而睿足焉，以之徧物而知足焉。是惟無感，而感之斯通，凡以式百官而御萬民者，將無事自用而有餘裕矣。其諸日月之重明麗天，而照臨于無外乎？夫生知之質具，而知臨之宜得如此，由是四德之良皆從此出，而以容、以執、以敬、以別，莫非有臨之資矣。非天下之至聖，其孰能與于斯哉？雖然，生知至堯舜極矣。書紀堯之欽明、舜之濬哲，而必繼之允恭允塞，蓋有誠敬之實，而後生知可充也。况乎孔子告哀公以誠之之功，而終之以雖愚必明，氣質之不足恃且拘也審矣。故曰：「人主務聰明之實。」

其爲氣也，至大至剛，以直養而無害，則塞
translation_en:
…within a single heart; thus, what enables him to illuminate the four quarters is drawn from profound subtlety and is sufficient in itself. He unites illumination and wisdom to establish a standard; thus, what enables him to rule the myriad states draws upon what he preserves in stillness and is more than sufficient. Through this, his acuity suffices to hear all sides, and his clarity suffices to survey all things. Though its operation is hidden, it becomes manifest when employed. In managing the myriad affairs of government and presiding over all activity, he will have sufficient resources within himself without resorting to contrived action. Is this not like Heaven’s radiance reaching down below and shedding light in every direction without limit? Through this, his sagacity suffices to ponder subtleties, and his understanding suffices to encompass all things. Though unstirred, when stirred it responds with thorough comprehension. In setting a model for the hundred officials and governing the myriad people, he will have ample capacity without needing to insist upon his own judgment. Is this not like the combined brilliance of sun and moon attached to Heaven, illuminating everything without exception?

Thus endowed with the innate capacity to know, he attains in this manner the proper exercise of understanding in ruling others. From this source emerge all the excellences of the four virtues: his capacity to accommodate, to hold firm, to show reverence, and to distinguish—all provide resources for his rule. Who but the utmost sage under Heaven could attain this? Nevertheless, innate knowledge reached its highest point in Yao and Shun. The Book of Documents records Yao’s reverent illumination and Shun’s profound wisdom, yet necessarily follows these with genuine reverence and genuine integrity. Only with the substance of sincerity and reverence can innate knowledge be fully developed. Moreover, Kongzi instructed Duke Ai in the work of making oneself sincere and concluded that even the foolish would surely become clear-sighted. It is therefore evident that one’s psychophysical endowment is insufficient to rely upon and can also constrain one. Hence the saying: “The ruler must strive for the substance of acuity and clarity.”

As for this vital force, it is supremely great and supremely unyielding. If nourished with uprightness and left unharmed, it fills…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
于天地之間其爲氣也配義與道無是
餒也是集義所生者非義襲而取之也
行有不慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未
甞知義以其外之也必有事焉而勿正
心勿忘勿助長也
高士儆
同考試官教諭孟　批〔辭簡理足且莊嚴中有順題錯綜者在心思筆力俱到宜錄以式〕
考試官教諭張　批〔渾融充倢是養浩然有得者〕
===
考試官學正高　批〔善發孟子之藴〕
大賢詳論浩然之氣惟在所養而已矣甚矣氣
本浩然也善養之則塞天地而配道義矣集義
養氣之功寧容已哉孟子告公孫丑之意若曰
浩然之氣固難言矣然豈終無可言耶吾甞反
而觀之但見其爲氣也至大而不可禦焉至剛
而無所撓焉蓋天地與我之正氣也人患無以
養之耳苟能直養而無以害之則氣之剛大者
適得吾體自與天地相似而充塞之無間矣豈
punctuated:
于天地之間。其爲氣也，配義與道；無是，餒也。是集義所生者，非義襲而取之也。行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰告子未甞知義，以其外之也。必有事焉而勿正，心勿忘，勿助長也。

高士儆

同考試官教諭孟，批〔辭簡理足，且莊嚴中有順題錯綜者在，心思筆力俱到，宜錄以式。〕

考試官教諭張，批〔渾融充倢，是養浩然有得者。〕

考試官學正高，批〔善發孟子之藴。〕

大賢詳論浩然之氣，惟在所養而已矣。甚矣，氣本浩然也！善養之，則塞天地而配道義矣。集義養氣之功，寧容已哉？孟子告公孫丑之意若曰：浩然之氣固難言矣，然豈終無可言耶？吾甞反而觀之，但見其爲氣也，至大而不可禦焉，至剛而無所撓焉，蓋天地與我之正氣也。人患無以養之耳。苟能直養而無以害之，則氣之剛大者適得吾體，自與天地相似，而充塞之無間矣。豈
translation_en:
…between Heaven and Earth. This qi accords with righteousness and the Way; without these, it starves. It is produced by accumulating righteous deeds, not acquired through an isolated act of righteousness. If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, it starves. Thus I say that Gaozi has never understood righteousness, because he regards it as external. One must keep working at it without anticipating the result; the heart must neither forget it nor help it grow by force.

Gao Shijing 高士儆

Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor, comments: 〔The language is concise and the reasoning sufficient. Within its dignified presentation, it follows the topic while interweaving its themes. Both thought and literary execution are fully accomplished. It should be recorded as a model.〕

Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Harmoniously integrated and amply accomplished [?]: this is the work of someone who has attained an understanding of nurturing the vast, flowing qi.〕

Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: 〔It skillfully brings out the deeper meaning of Mengzi’s teaching.〕

The great worthy’s detailed discussion of the vast, flowing qi concerns nothing other than its nurture. How profoundly vast and flowing qi is by nature! Nurture it well, and it fills Heaven and Earth and accords with the Way and righteousness. How could one cease the work of accumulating righteous deeds and nurturing qi? The meaning of Mengzi’s words to Gongsun Chou is as follows: The vast, flowing qi is indeed difficult to describe, but can there ultimately be nothing to say about it? I have turned inward and examined it, and I see only that this qi is supremely great and cannot be resisted, supremely firm and cannot be bent. It is the upright qi shared by Heaven and Earth and myself. The trouble is simply that people lack the means to nurture it. If one can nurture it with uprightness and do nothing to harm it, then this firm and great qi finds its proper place in my person. Of itself, it accords with Heaven and Earth and fills them without a gap. Could it…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
特爲體之充耶氣之流行者不失吾常道義所
在自相資而互發矣苟無是氣道義豈可以虛
行耶夫氣之養成也如此然養也何如哉葢
必精義之功已得於積累之久是以浩然之氣
自生於養盛之餘耳固非可以襲取於外而得
之也若行一不得於心則氣自不充於體矣義
豈在外乎彼告子以義爲外者正不知所謂義
也亦安知所謂集哉是故善養氣者要必以集
義爲事而所以戒襲求慊者務事事之合宜至
===
於效之未臻也則不可先焉其或未充也尤必
以集義爲心而所以去餒思充者惟亹亹而匪
懈至於功之未致也則不可强焉夫有事勿忘
旣盡夫直養之功勿正勿助又無所謂作爲之
害如是而剛大之氣自全於我矣尚何天地之
不塞而道義之不配哉抑論性不論氣不備葢
性者天地之原而道義之統也理氣相須所以
塞而配之者氣之能也所以集而養之者理之
宰也然則善養氣者固所以善養其性歟彼告
punctuated: 特爲體之充耶？氣之流行者，不失吾常，道義所在，自相資而互發矣。苟無是氣，道義豈可以虛行耶？夫氣之養成也如此，然養也何如哉？葢必精義之功，已得於積累之久，是以浩然之氣，自生於養盛之餘耳，固非可以襲取於外而得之也。若行一不得於心，則氣自不充於體矣。義豈在外乎？彼告子以義爲外者，正不知所謂義也，亦安知所謂集哉？是故善養氣者，要必以集義爲事，而所以戒襲求慊者，務事事之合宜。至於效之未臻也，則不可先焉。其或未充也，尤必以集義爲心，而所以去餒思充者，惟亹亹而匪懈。至於功之未致也，則不可强焉。夫有事勿忘，旣盡夫直養之功；勿正勿助，又無所謂作爲之害。如是而剛大之氣，自全於我矣。尚何天地之不塞，而道義之不配哉？抑論性不論氣，不備。葢性者，天地之原，而道義之統也。理氣相須，所以塞而配之者，氣之能也；所以集而養之者，理之宰也。然則善養氣者，固所以善養其性歟？彼告
translation_en:
…merely fill the body? As this qi circulates, it does not depart from our constant nature; wherever the Way and righteousness reside, they and qi sustain and bring forth one another. Without this qi, how could the Way and righteousness operate in emptiness? Such is qi when its cultivation is complete. But how is it cultivated? Only after the work of discerning righteousness precisely has accumulated over a long period does flood-like qi arise naturally from abundant cultivation. It certainly cannot be obtained by seizing it from outside. If even one action fails to satisfy the heart, qi will of itself fail to fill the body. How could righteousness lie outside? Gaozi, who regarded righteousness as external, simply did not understand what righteousness means. How, then, could he understand what it means to accumulate it?

Thus, those who cultivate qi well must make the accumulation of righteousness their task. To guard against seizing it through an isolated act and to seek satisfaction in the heart, they strive to make every action fitting. If the effects have not yet been attained, however, they must not anticipate them. If qi is still not full, they must all the more set their hearts on accumulating righteousness. To dispel its depletion and seek its fullness, they must work diligently without slackening. If their efforts have not yet reached fruition, however, they must not force the result. By keeping to their task and never forgetting it, they fully accomplish the work of nourishing qi with uprightness; by neither fixing upon a result nor helping its growth along, they also avoid the harm of contrived intervention. In this way, firm and expansive qi becomes complete within us of itself. How could it then fail to fill Heaven and Earth and accord with the Way and righteousness?

Moreover, to discuss human nature without discussing qi is incomplete. Human nature is the source of Heaven and Earth and the unifying principle of the Way and righteousness. Principle and qi depend upon one another. What fills Heaven and Earth and accords with the Way and righteousness is the capacity of qi; what accumulates righteousness and nourishes qi is the governing power of principle. Thus, is cultivating qi well not precisely the means of cultivating one’s nature well? As for Gao…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
子不得於心勿求於氣至於杞柳湍水之喻起
指氣之失養者爲性焉寧不暴氣而害性乎噫
此孟子所以好辨也
易
當位以節中正以通
戴廷禮
同考試官教諭彭　批〔節天下之道在位與德之全而德尤其本作者往往拘兩平說此作大旨歸重于德蓋知要之言也取之〕
===
考試官教諭張　批〔認理精切措詞典雅〕
考試官學正高　批〔簡當可式〕
卦具君人之節而德以行之見其所由亨也夫
節必以位而德所以行之也卦體爲能兼隆焉
節之亨也宜哉象傳本卦藴以明亨也意謂聖
人之所貴于節者謂其坊天下之流而救其弊
也但以立節者係于位以善節者係于德兹于
卦體備之矣卦惟九五居乎尊位而有中正之
德焉是其陟元后以臨民盡天下而皆歸于統
punctuated:
子不得於心，勿求於氣，至於杞柳湍水之喻起，指氣之失養者爲性焉，寧不暴氣而害性乎？噫！此孟子所以好辨也。

易
當位以節，中正以通。
戴廷禮
同考試官教諭彭　批〔節天下之道，在位與德之全，而德尤其本。作者往往拘兩平說，此作大旨歸重于德，蓋知要之言也。取之。〕
考試官教諭張　批〔認理精切，措詞典雅。〕
考試官學正高　批〔簡當可式。〕

卦具君人之節，而德以行之，見其所由亨也。夫節必以位，而德所以行之也。卦體爲能兼隆焉，節之亨也宜哉！象傳本卦藴以明亨也，意謂聖人之所貴于節者，謂其坊天下之流而救其弊也。但以立節者係于位，以善節者係于德，兹于卦體備之矣。卦惟九五居乎尊位，而有中正之德焉。是其陟元后以臨民，盡天下而皆歸于統
translation_en:
…Gaozi held that what one does not obtain in the heart should not be sought in vital energy. When he advanced his analogies of willow wood and swirling water, he identified vital energy deprived of proper nourishment as human nature. Was this not to abuse vital energy and injure human nature? Alas! This is why Mencius was fond of disputation.

Book of Changes
“Occupying the proper position to impose limitation; being central and correct to achieve free passage.”
Dai Tingli

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor: 〔The way to regulate all under Heaven requires the completeness of both position and virtue, but virtue is especially its foundation. Writers are often constrained to discuss the two with equal emphasis. The main purport of this composition places the weight on virtue: these are indeed the words of someone who understands the essential point. Accept it.〕
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔His grasp of principle is precise and penetrating; his diction is refined and elegant.〕
Comment by Examiner Gao, Instructor: 〔Concise and apt; worthy of serving as a model.〕

The hexagram embodies the regulation proper to a ruler of men, and virtue puts it into practice: here we see the source of its success. Regulation necessarily depends on position, while virtue is what carries it into effect. The structure of the hexagram brings both to their fullest expression. How fitting that Limitation should bring success! The Commentary on the Images draws upon the meaning contained in the hexagram to explain this success. Its meaning is that what the sage values in regulation is its ability to check the wayward currents of the world and remedy their harmful effects. Yet establishing regulations depends on position, while regulating well depends on virtue; both are fully present in the structure of this hexagram. Within it, the nine in the fifth place occupies the honored position and possesses the virtue of centrality and correctness. Thus he ascends to the position of sovereign to preside over the people, and all under Heaven comes under his governance…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
馭之內總乾剛以獨斷舉斯世而咸囿于宰制
之中由是秉此可節之權以立乎經世之法數
度自我制焉惟所範圍而不能外也德行自我
議焉惟所命令而不能違也此則天王爲紀法
之宗而位之所在其節也非天下之所共仰者
乎且非徒以其位已也緣大中以立極而措之
經綸適得乎宜民之術本至正以作則而章之
軌物丕昭乎盡制之休由是以此善節之道而
協夫人心之宜數度之制民咸用焉而推之無
===
不準也德行之議人共守焉而達之無不順也
此則天子建中和之極而道之所在其節也非
天下之所通行者乎夫以節而至于通亨孰尚
焉推其所自固本于德位之兼全而德尤其要
矣聖人示辭之意微矣哉抑是節也于義爲止
道在節天下而不過也且必本諸中正而後可
行焉況于一時之規畫與天下增益于經常之
外苟不揆諸中正之原而謂惟其所得爲將何
以示天下而導之從乎噫是不可不慎也然中
punctuated:
馭之內，總乾剛以獨斷，舉斯世而咸囿于宰制之中。由是秉此可節之權，以立乎經世之法。數度自我制焉，惟所範圍而不能外也；德行自我議焉，惟所命令而不能違也。此則天王爲紀法之宗，而位之所在，其節也非天下之所共仰者乎？且非徒以其位已也，緣大中以立極，而措之經綸，適得乎宜民之術；本至正以作則，而章之軌物，丕昭乎盡制之休。由是以此善節之道，而協夫人心之宜。數度之制，民咸用焉，而推之無不準也；德行之議，人共守焉，而達之無不順也。此則天子建中和之極，而道之所在，其節也非天下之所通行者乎？夫以節而至于通亨，孰尚焉？推其所自，固本于德位之兼全，而德尤其要矣。聖人示辭之意微矣哉！

抑是節也，于義爲止，道在節天下而不過也，且必本諸中正而後可行焉。況于一時之規畫，與天下增益于經常之外，苟不揆諸中正之原，而謂惟其所得爲，將何以示天下而導之從乎？噫！是不可不慎也。然中
translation_en:
…within his governance. He commands the firm strength of Heaven and decides alone, bringing this entire age within his rule. Thus he holds the authority to impose restraints and establishes laws for ordering the world. Numerical standards and measures are established by him: all must remain within the bounds he prescribes and cannot go beyond them. Virtuous conduct is deliberated upon by him: all must follow his commands and cannot contravene them. Thus the heavenly king is the source of norms and laws. Given his position, are his restraints not what all under Heaven look up to together? Nor is this merely a matter of his position. Following the great mean, he establishes the supreme standard; applying it to the ordering of affairs, he finds precisely the means suited to the people. Grounding himself in utmost correctness, he makes rules; manifesting them in standards of conduct, he splendidly displays the excellence of fully established institutions. Thus, through this way of imposing restraints well, he accords with what is fitting to people’s hearts. The people all employ the numerical standards and measures he establishes, and wherever these are extended, they serve as a true standard. Everyone observes his determinations concerning virtuous conduct, and wherever these reach, all accord with them. Thus the Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of centrality and harmony. Given the Way he embodies, are his restraints not universally practiced throughout the realm? When restraint achieves unhindered success, what could surpass it? Tracing its source, we find that it is indeed rooted in the full possession of both virtue and position, with virtue especially essential. How subtle is the sage’s meaning in setting forth these words!

Moreover, restraint means stopping: its Way lies in restraining all under Heaven without going too far. It must be grounded in centrality and correctness before it can be put into practice. How much more is this so with plans devised for a particular time, adding arrangements for the realm beyond its enduring norms! If one does not assess these by the underlying principle of centrality and correctness, but considers only what one has the power to do, how can one set an example for all under Heaven and guide them to follow? Alas! This demands the utmost care. Yet centrality…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
正之道豈易言哉精一以執中無爲以守正此
帝王相傳之要法皆自心焉求之也
黄帝堯舜垂衣裳而天下治
高士儆
同考試官教諭彭　批〔三聖神化無爲之妙豈以衣裳之〕
〔制出于通變非强作也此作直探邃古而詞意足以發之真潜心于易〕
〔學者取之〕
考試官教諭張　批〔識精詞雅迥異常作〕
考試官學正高　批〔純正〕
===
大傳論三聖興文明之化而變通之妙見矣葢
衣裳之制文教之始也三聖興之而天下化成
焉不可以見通變之妙哉大傳明聖人制器尚
象之事及此葢謂聖人之治與天下相安于無
爲者其心也而不容不有所爲者時也時之所
宜而與民通之則亦無爲而已矣昔者黄帝堯
舜之繼神農而王也風氣雖漸闢矣而朴陋之
尚存天下不能無變革之心法制雖漸備矣而
文教之未興人情不能無更化之願三聖本風
punctuated:
正之道，豈易言哉！精一以執中，無爲以守正，此帝王相傳之要法，皆自心焉求之也。

黄帝堯舜垂衣裳而天下治
高士儆
同考試官教諭彭，批〔三聖神化無爲之妙，豈以衣裳之〕〔制出于通變，非强作也。此作直探邃古，而詞意足以發之，真潜心于易〕〔學者，取之。〕
考試官教諭張，批〔識精詞雅，迥異常作。〕
考試官學正高，批〔純正。〕

大傳論三聖興文明之化，而變通之妙見矣。葢衣裳之制，文教之始也。三聖興之，而天下化成焉，不可以見通變之妙哉？大傳明聖人制器尚象之事，及此，葢謂聖人之治，與天下相安于無爲者，其心也；而不容不有所爲者，時也。時之所宜，而與民通之，則亦無爲而已矣。昔者黄帝堯舜之繼神農而王也，風氣雖漸闢矣，而朴陋之尚存，天下不能無變革之心；法制雖漸備矣，而文教之未興，人情不能無更化之願。三聖本風
translation_en:
…the Way of centrality and correctness—how could it be easy to explain! To remain discerning and single-minded so as to hold to the mean, and to practice nonaction so as to preserve correctness: these are the essential methods transmitted from one sage sovereign to another, all to be sought within the heart.

“ Huangdi, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down, and all under Heaven was governed.”
Gao Shijing

Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor, comments: “The marvel of the three sages’ numinous transformation through nonaction—could it be through their garments… [?] The institution arose from adapting to change, rather than from forced contrivance. This composition probes directly into remote antiquity, and its language and ideas suffice to elucidate it. Truly the work of someone who has devoted himself to studying the Changes; accept it.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “Discerning in understanding and elegant in expression; far beyond ordinary compositions.”
Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: “Pure and orthodox.”

The Great Commentary discusses how the three sages initiated the transforming influence of cultural refinement, revealing the marvel of adaptation to change. The institution of upper and lower garments was the beginning of cultural instruction. The three sages established it, and all under Heaven was transformed and brought to completion. Does this not reveal the marvel of adapting to change? In elucidating how the sages fashioned implements by taking the images as their models, the Great Commentary reaches this matter. Its meaning is that, in governing, the sages intended to dwell in mutual peace with all under Heaven through nonaction; yet the times made it impossible for them to refrain entirely from action. By making what suited the times generally available to the people, they were still simply practicing nonaction.

Long ago, when Huangdi, Yao, and Shun succeeded Shennong as rulers, prevailing customs had gradually become more enlightened, yet primitive crudity remained, so people throughout the realm could not but harbor thoughts of change. Laws and institutions had gradually become more complete, yet cultural instruction had not arisen, so people could not but wish for renewed transformation. The three sages took as their basis the prevailing currents…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
會之所趨而象服之制創焉質極而示之以文
初非强人以不欲也緣羣情之所向而華飾之
章立焉儉極而導之以禮初非容心以紛更也
由是以辨上下則禮讓之風斯興舉天下鄙陋
之習而相率于雍容之美有不知誰之所爲矣
以别等威而文爲之盛斯著舉一世渾樸之俗
而相忘于熙明之天有不知帝之爲力矣我無
所爲而四方恊從欲之治風俗自是其可同矣
所謂一通變而民不倦焉非以此哉上無所作
而萬邦成於變之化治教自是其休明矣所謂
一神化而民自宜焉不以是哉謂之曰垂衣裳
而天下治信乎一乾坤變化而無爲也三聖所
以繼天立極者蓋如此雖然天下有得與民變
革者制也有不得與民變革者道也三聖衣裳
之制猶之網罟耒耜而已乃其河圖之受精一
執中之旨上遡羲皇之秘下垂道統之傳夫寧
有二哉厥後非天子不制度而欲制度者其可
不求諸道乎
punctuated:
會之所趨，而象服之制創焉。質極而示之以文，初非强人以不欲也。緣羣情之所向，而華飾之章立焉。儉極而導之以禮，初非容心以紛更也。由是以辨上下，則禮讓之風斯興，舉天下鄙陋之習，而相率于雍容之美，有不知誰之所爲矣。以别等威，而文爲之盛斯著，舉一世渾樸之俗，而相忘于熙明之天，有不知帝之爲力矣。我無所爲，而四方恊從欲之治，風俗自是其可同矣。所謂一通變而民不倦焉，非以此哉？上無所作，而萬邦成於變之化，治教自是其休明矣。所謂一神化而民自宜焉，不以是哉？謂之曰「垂衣裳而天下治」，信乎一乾坤變化而無爲也。三聖所以繼天立極者，蓋如此。
雖然，天下有得與民變革者，制也；有不得與民變革者，道也。三聖衣裳之制，猶之網罟耒耜而已。乃其河圖之受、精一執中之旨，上遡羲皇之秘，下垂道統之傳，夫寧有二哉？厥後，非天子不制度，而欲制度者，其可不求諸道乎？
translation_en:
…the direction in which the circumstances of the age were tending, and thus the system of emblematic robes was created. When plainness had reached its limit, they displayed refinement to the people; they never intended to force upon people what they did not desire. Following the inclinations of the multitude, they established the prescribed forms of splendid adornment. When frugality had reached its limit, they guided the people through ritual; they never intended to introduce a confusion of changes merely at their own whim. By distinguishing those above from those below, they fostered a spirit of ritual propriety and deference. Throughout the realm, people left their crude habits behind and led one another toward the beauty of dignified ease, without knowing who had brought this about. By distinguishing ranks and their corresponding dignities, they made the richness of ceremonial forms manifest. An entire age’s unhewn simplicity gave way to an unselfconscious life beneath a bright and harmonious heaven, without people knowing that the sovereign’s efforts had brought it about. “I take no action,” yet the four quarters harmoniously follow the desired order; from this point, customs can be brought into accord. Is this not what is meant by saying that, once change is accommodated, the people do not grow weary? Those above undertake no contrivance, yet the myriad states achieve transformation; from this point, government and instruction become splendid and enlightened. Is this not what is meant by saying that, once transformation works with spiritual efficacy, the people naturally find what suits them? It is called “letting the robes and skirts hang down, and the realm is ordered.” Truly, this is wholly at one with the transformations of Qian and Kun—Heaven and Earth—and acts without contrivance. Such, indeed, was how the Three Sages continued Heaven’s work and established the supreme standard.
Nevertheless, there is something in the realm that may be changed together with the people: institutions. There is something that may not be changed together with the people: the Way. The Three Sages’ system of robes and skirts was, in this respect, merely like nets and ploughs. But as for the reception of the River Chart and the teaching of refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to the Mean—tracing back to the mysteries of the sovereign Fuxi and handing down the succession of the Way to later generations—could these ever have been two different things? Thereafter, none but the Son of Heaven might establish institutions and regulations. Could anyone wishing to establish them fail to seek their foundation in the Way?

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
書
后克艱厥后臣克艱厥臣政乃乂黎民敏
德帝曰俞允若茲嘉言罔攸伏野無遺
賢萬邦咸寧
邢鳳毛
同考試官教諭謝　批〔治至虞廷爲極乃其君臣交儆于克艱之義正聖人無窮之心也此作闡明殆盡其神契〕
聖謨者哉宜式多士
考試官教諭張　批〔發都俞之意藹然〕
===
考試官學正高　批〔明淨雅健宜冠本房〕
大臣言君臣盡道之效聖君契其言而廣其效
焉蓋君臣萬化之原也誠能各盡其道而效之
所致不亦廣乎宜大臣言之而聖君契之也且
昔有虞之世君明臣良治隆化洽矣然大禹圖
治之心未已也乃言于帝曰王天下之治者后
也而后道唯艱矣輔天下之治者臣也而臣職
不易矣必也欲爲君盡君道而代天之責兢兢
焉期以克舉之也欲爲臣盡臣道而代終之義
punctuated:
書

后克艱厥后，臣克艱厥臣，政乃乂，黎民敏德。帝曰：「俞！允若茲，嘉言罔攸伏，野無遺賢，萬邦咸寧。」

邢鳳毛

同考試官教諭謝批〔治至虞廷爲極，乃其君臣交儆于克艱之義，正聖人無窮之心也。此作闡明殆盡，其神契〕聖謨者哉！宜式多士。

考試官教諭張批〔發都俞之意，藹然。〕

考試官學正高批〔明淨雅健，宜冠本房。〕

大臣言君臣盡道之效，聖君契其言而廣其效焉。蓋君臣萬化之原也，誠能各盡其道，而效之所致，不亦廣乎？宜大臣言之而聖君契之也。且昔有虞之世，君明臣良，治隆化洽矣。然大禹圖治之心未已也，乃言于帝曰：「王天下之治者，后也，而后道唯艱矣；輔天下之治者，臣也，而臣職不易矣。必也欲爲君盡君道，而代天之責，兢兢焉期以克舉之也；欲爲臣盡臣道，而代終之義
translation_en:
Book of Documents

“When the ruler can recognize the difficulty of being a ruler, and ministers can recognize the difficulty of being ministers, government will be well ordered and the common people diligent in virtue.” The emperor said: “Yes! If it is truly thus, no worthy words will remain concealed, no worthy men will be left undiscovered in the countryside, and the myriad states will all enjoy peace.”

Xing Fengmao

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor: 〔“Government reached its highest perfection at the court of Yu. Yet its ruler and ministers admonished one another about recognizing the difficulty of their duties: this precisely expresses the sage’s inexhaustible concern. This composition expounds the matter almost fully. Surely its spirit accords with〕 the counsels of the sages! It should serve as a model for the many scholars.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔“It unfolds the meaning of those exclamations of praise and assent with abundant warmth.”〕

Comment by Examiner Gao, Instructor: 〔“Clear, lucid, elegant, and vigorous: it deserves first place in this examining section.”〕

A great minister speaks of the effects of ruler and ministers fully fulfilling their respective ways; the sage ruler accords with his words and extends those effects. For ruler and ministers are the source of all transforming influences. If each can truly fulfill his own way, will not the resulting effects be far-reaching? It is fitting that the great minister should speak of this and the sage ruler agree with him.

Now, in the age of Yu, the ruler was enlightened and his ministers worthy; government flourished and moral transformation reached everywhere. Yet the Great Yu’s resolve to achieve good government remained unceasing. He therefore said to the emperor: “It is the ruler who governs all under Heaven as sovereign, and the ruler’s way is indeed difficult. It is ministers who assist in governing all under Heaven, and their duties are not easy. Whoever wishes to be a ruler must fully fulfill the ruler’s way and, with vigilant care, seek to discharge the responsibility of acting on Heaven’s behalf. Whoever wishes to be a minister must fully fulfill the minister’s way, and the duty of bringing undertakings to completion on the ruler’s behalf…”

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
業業焉求以克勝之也君臣克艱如此吾見脩
政之功足以振精明之治而綱舉目張上無不
乂之政矣化民之術足以速觀感之機而遷善
協中下皆敏德之民矣豈非效之必至者哉然
大禹祇承之心即帝舜保治之心也於是帝聞
其言而俞之曰德業成於上下之交事功起於
明良之會信能克艱其效豈但已哉將見延納
既廣而嘉謀起樂告之誠善無不言無不盡
也寧有隱伏者耶明揚有道而黎獻遂登庸之
===
願知無不舉舉無不先也奚有遺佚者耶道化
孚而兆民得所膏澤究而天下舉安萬邦奚有
弗寧者耶蓋至是而政乂民化之效益廣矣豈
非君臣克艱之所致哉是則大禹之誤責難之
敬也帝舜之言樂取之誠也虞廷都俞之盛如
此此其治之不可及歟抑舜禹君臣艱罔弗克
治罔弗隆而其相戒之辭恒惴惴若不及者是
豈作而致其情哉其心誠以天下至廣萬民至
衆有一不得其所皆予責也故曰危微曰儆戒
punctuated: 業業焉求以克勝之也。君臣克艱如此，吾見脩政之功足以振精明之治，而綱舉目張，上無不乂之政矣；化民之術足以速觀感之機，而遷善協中，下皆敏德之民矣。豈非效之必至者哉？」然大禹祇承之心，即帝舜保治之心也。於是帝聞其言而俞之曰：「德業成於上下之交，事功起於明良之會。信能克艱，其效豈但已哉？將見延納既廣，而嘉謀起樂告之誠，善無不言，言無不盡也，寧有隱伏者耶？明揚有道，而黎獻遂登庸之願，知無不舉，舉無不先也，奚有遺佚者耶？道化孚而兆民得所，膏澤究而天下舉安，萬邦奚有弗寧者耶？」蓋至是而政乂民化之效益廣矣，豈非君臣克艱之所致哉？是則大禹之誤，責難之敬也；帝舜之言，樂取之誠也。虞廷都俞之盛如此，此其治之不可及歟？抑舜禹君臣，艱罔弗克，治罔弗隆，而其相戒之辭恒惴惴若不及者，是豈作而致其情哉？其心誠以天下至廣，萬民至衆，有一不得其所，皆予責也。故曰危微，曰儆戒，
translation_en:
…and, with trembling vigilance, seek to prove equal to that duty. When ruler and ministers thus overcome their difficulties, I see that their work of improving government will suffice to invigorate enlightened rule: the guiding cords will be raised and every mesh set in order, so that above, no affair of government remains unregulated. Their methods of transforming the people will suffice to hasten the response inspired by observing good examples: the people will turn toward goodness and accord with the mean, so that below, all will be diligent in virtue. Are these not results that must surely follow?”

Yet the reverence with which the Great Yu undertook his duties was precisely the concern with which Emperor Shun preserved good government. Thus, hearing his words, the emperor assented and said: “Virtuous achievement is accomplished through communion between those above and those below; practical accomplishments arise from the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers. If they can indeed overcome their difficulties, how could the effects stop there? We shall see that, once invitations and access have been extended widely, excellent counsel will spring from a sincere delight in offering advice. No good idea will go unspoken, and nothing spoken will remain incompletely expressed. Could anything remain concealed? When the discerning promotion of worthy men follows the proper way, the worthies among the people will fulfill their desire to enter service. None who are known will go unrecommended, and none recommended will fail to receive precedence. Could any worthy remain overlooked? When moral transformation wins trust, the myriad people will find their proper places; when beneficence reaches everywhere, all under Heaven will enjoy peace. Could any of the myriad states remain unsettled?”

At this point, the effects of orderly government and the transformation of the people become still more extensive. Is this not brought about by ruler and ministers overcoming their difficulties? Thus the Great Yu’s words [?] express the reverence of one who calls upon his ruler to accomplish difficult things, while Emperor Shun’s words express his sincere delight in accepting good counsel. Such was the flourishing exchange of praise and assent at the court of Yu: was this why its government could not be equaled? Moreover, as ruler and minister, Shun and Yu overcame every difficulty and brought government to the height of flourishing. Yet in their words of mutual admonition they were always anxious, as though falling short. Could this have been a contrived expression of feeling? In their hearts they truly thought: “All under Heaven is so vast, and its people so numerous; if even one fails to find a proper place, the responsibility is mine.” Hence they spoke of peril and subtlety, and of vigilance and admonition…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
曰兢業其言不同其旨則一矣故曰聖人之心
無窮又曰聖人不以吾治爲已足有以哉
穆穆在上明明在下灼于四方
張允升
同考試官教諭謝　批〔虞廷君臣去此時遠矣呂刑〕〔若追敘之詞此作形容穆穆明明宛乎面𧟌且文詞典則非〕
凡格此取之
考試官欽諭張　批〔不襲時套雅有矩度〕
考試官學正高　批〔精切不浮〕
===
聖世君臣德容之盛而達於無閒者也蓋穆穆
明明德之著於容者盛矣而光輝四達焉自非
虞世君臣能如是乎宜穆王申言以訓刑也蓋
謂聖人之御世也不徒任法以維治而惟尚德
以化民吾嘗上嘉有虞而想見其盛矣是故穆
穆者和敬之容也惟帝舜之爲君也而德威德
明焉則純粹之懿著之爲雍肅之儀大和洋溢
藹乎其可親也至敬流通儼乎其可象也在上
何穆穆乎明明者精白之容也今三后之爲臣
punctuated:
曰兢業，其言不同，其旨則一矣。故曰：「聖人之心無窮。」又曰：「聖人不以吾治爲已足。」有以哉！

穆穆在上，明明在下，灼于四方。
張允升
同考試官教諭謝　批〔虞廷君臣去此時遠矣，呂刑〕〔若追敘之詞，此作形容穆穆明明，宛乎面𧟌，且文詞典則，非〕凡格，此取之。
考試官欽諭張　批〔不襲時套，雅有矩度。〕
考試官學正高　批〔精切不浮。〕

聖世君臣德容之盛，而達於無閒者也。蓋穆穆明明，德之著於容者盛矣，而光輝四達焉。自非虞世君臣，能如是乎？宜穆王申言以訓刑也。蓋謂聖人之御世也，不徒任法以維治，而惟尚德以化民。吾嘗上嘉有虞，而想見其盛矣。是故穆穆者，和敬之容也。惟帝舜之爲君也，而德威德明焉，則純粹之懿著之爲雍肅之儀，大和洋溢，藹乎其可親也；至敬流通，儼乎其可象也。在上何穆穆乎！明明者，精白之容也。今三后之爲臣
translation_en:
…and speak of being watchful and diligent. Their words differ, but their purport is one. Thus it is said, “The sage’s concern has no limit,” and again, “The sage does not consider his own governance sufficient.” These sayings indeed have their reasons!

“Solemn and reverent above, discerning and enlightened below, their radiance shone throughout the four quarters.”
By Zhang Yunsheng.

Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor, comments: “The ruler and ministers of the court of Yu were far removed from this time. The ‘Punishments of Lü’ seems to recount them retrospectively. This composition depicts their solemn reverence and enlightened discernment as though they were before one’s very eyes [?]. Moreover, its language is classical and disciplined, exceeding the ordinary standard. For these reasons I select it.”
Examiner Zhang, whose title is transcribed as qinyu 欽諭 [?], comments: “It does not copy the conventional formulas of the day, and possesses elegant discipline.”
Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: “Precise and incisive, without superficiality.”

This speaks of the flourishing virtue and bearing of ruler and ministers in a sage age, extending everywhere without interruption. For solemn reverence and enlightened discernment are virtue abundantly manifested in outward bearing, its radiance reaching in all four directions. Who but the ruler and ministers of the age of Yu could have attained this? It was fitting that King Mu should reiterate this in his instructions concerning punishments.

His meaning was that, in governing the world, a sage does not merely rely on laws to maintain order, but esteems virtue above all to transform the people. “I have long looked back in admiration upon Youyu and pictured its flourishing age.” Thus, solemn reverence is the outward bearing of harmony and respect. As ruler, Emperor Shun inspired awe through virtue and illumined through virtue. The excellence of his unalloyed virtue manifested itself in a dignified and harmonious bearing. Supreme harmony brimmed over, making him gracious and approachable; utmost reverence permeated his conduct, making him imposing and worthy of emulation. How solemn and reverent he was above! Enlightened discernment is the outward bearing of purity and clarity. Now, as for the three lords serving as ministers…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
也而恤功于民焉則憂勤之心彰之爲昭融之
象勵精煥發而熙載者日宣也明作奮揚而亮
工者日嚴也在下何明明乎君臣之德徵諸容
者如此由是有道之氣象自宣夫赫奕之休而
合四方以勸施初不見其或禦令德之威儀自
著夫輝煌之盛而盡四表以光被殆不見其或
遺和敬形于一人而英華達於四訖自邇以及
遠旁燭其無疆焉浩浩乎遍及之神何者不在
其文明之中乎精白凝於羣后而光輝至於四
===
敷由中以達外於昭其無間焉蕩蕩乎廣運之
妙何者不在其照臨之下乎吁此君臣昭德以
化民殆有出於法制之外而不徒恃乎刑者矣
典獄者其尚鑒之抑帝王之治法天者也天之
道先陽而後陰故聖之治先德而後刑而協中
之化萬古稱隆焉後世任法律而不知有仁義
者不罪於帝王寧不媿於呂刑乎此呂刑之所
以見録於書也
詩
punctuated:
也，而恤功于民焉，則憂勤之心彰之爲昭融之象，勵精煥發而熙載者日宣也，明作奮揚而亮工者日嚴也。在下何明明乎！君臣之德徵諸容者如此，由是有道之氣象自宣夫赫奕之休，而合四方以勸施，初不見其或禦；令德之威儀自著夫輝煌之盛，而盡四表以光被，殆不見其或遺。和敬形于一人，而英華達於四訖，自邇以及遠，旁燭其無疆焉。浩浩乎遍及之神，何者不在其文明之中乎？精白凝於羣后，而光輝至於四敷，由中以達外，於昭其無間焉。蕩蕩乎廣運之妙，何者不在其照臨之下乎？吁！此君臣昭德以化民，殆有出於法制之外，而不徒恃乎刑者矣。典獄者其尚鑒之！抑帝王之治，法天者也。天之道先陽而後陰，故聖之治先德而後刑，而協中之化，萬古稱隆焉。後世任法律而不知有仁義者，不罪於帝王，寧不媿於《呂刑》乎？此《呂刑》之所以見録於《書》也。

《詩》
translation_en:
…and they concerned themselves with accomplishments benefiting the people. Their anxious diligence thus manifested itself in an appearance of luminous harmony. Rousing their energies to radiant activity, they daily made their advancement of affairs more evident; acting with discernment and exerting themselves, they daily became more exacting in fulfilling their duties. How illustrious they were in their subordinate stations! Such was the way the virtue of ruler and ministers was evidenced in their bearing. Thus the atmosphere of a realm possessing the Way naturally displayed its resplendent excellence, uniting the four quarters in encouragement to practice goodness, with no apparent resistance. The majestic bearing of excellent virtue naturally revealed its brilliant splendor, extending its light to the outermost bounds, seemingly leaving nothing untouched. Harmony and reverence took visible form in the sovereign, and their glorious essence reached the four limits [?], shining everywhere without bounds, from near to far. Vast was this all-pervading spiritual efficacy: what lay outside its civilizing radiance? Purity and integrity were concentrated in the assembled ministers, and their brilliance spread in all four directions, extending from within to without, shining without interruption. Boundless was the wondrous reach of this influence: what lay beyond its illumination? Ah! In making their virtue manifest to transform the people, this ruler and his ministers surely accomplished something beyond laws and institutions, rather than relying solely on punishments. May those responsible for judicial proceedings take this as their mirror! Moreover, the government of emperors and kings takes Heaven as its model. The Way of Heaven places yang before yin; hence the government of sages places virtue before punishment. Its transforming influence, in accord with the Mean, has therefore been acclaimed through all ages as supremely flourishing. Those of later ages who rely on laws without knowing benevolence and righteousness—even if they incur no condemnation from the emperors and kings, can they feel no shame before the “Punishments of Lü”? This is why the “Punishments of Lü” was included in the Book of Documents.

Book of Odes

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
鳲鳩在桑其子在棘淑人君子其儀不忒
其儀不忒正是四國
侯于曾
同考試官教諭李　批〔不忒正四國處場中類多浮泛可厭此作真切精當善形容風人之意是宜錄出〕
考試官教諭張　批〔體裁嚴整詞氣明亮正身率物之意儼然溢目蓋潛心於經學者〕
考試官學正高　批〔莊重溫雅〕
===
詩人美君子而與其身之為度焉蓋威儀者身
之章也君子有不忒之儀則可以為度矣謂不
足以正四國哉鳲鳩之詩美君子用心之善也
想其託興之意若曰心者萬化之原而身者四
方之極也吾茲有感於君子矣彼鳲鳩在桑其
子在棘焉是不以子而易其所止之常也在物
固有然者矣況我淑人君子耶本之以如結之
心既立夫大方外之體形而為有常之度自協乎
中正之觀施於四體不惟其儀之一也致禮以
punctuated:
鳲鳩在桑，其子在棘。淑人君子，其儀不忒。其儀不忒，正是四國。
侯于曾
同考試官教諭李，批〔不忒正四國處，場中類多浮泛可厭。此作真切精當，善形容風人之意，是宜錄出。〕
考試官教諭張，批〔體裁嚴整，詞氣明亮，正身率物之意，儼然溢目。蓋潛心於經學者。〕
考試官學正高，批〔莊重溫雅。〕
詩人美君子而與其身之為度焉。蓋威儀者，身之章也。君子有不忒之儀，則可以為度矣，謂不足以正四國哉？鳲鳩之詩，美君子用心之善也。想其託興之意，若曰：心者，萬化之原，而身者，四方之極也。吾茲有感於君子矣。彼鳲鳩在桑，其子在棘焉，是不以子而易其所止之常也。在物固有然者矣，況我淑人君子耶？本之以如結之心，既立夫大方外之體，形而為有常之度，自協乎中正之觀。施於四體，不惟其儀之一也，致禮以
translation_en:
“The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree; its young are in the thorn tree. The good man, the gentleman—his deportment does not err. His deportment does not err, and he sets right the states of the four quarters.”

Hou Yuzeng

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔In treating ‘does not err’ and ‘sets right the states of the four quarters,’ examination essays are generally so superficial and vague as to be tiresome. This composition is concrete, precise, and apt, and skillfully conveys the poet’s meaning. It deserves to be included in the record.〕

Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔The composition is rigorously structured, and its language and tone are clear and bright. The meaning of rectifying oneself and leading others stands vividly before the eyes. This must be the work of someone deeply devoted to classical learning.〕

Examiner Gao, Director of Studies, comments: 〔Dignified and composed, gentle and elegant.〕

The poet praises the gentleman and acknowledges that his own person serves as a standard. For dignified deportment is the outward manifestation of the person. When the gentleman’s deportment is without error, he can serve as a standard. Could one say that he is insufficient to set right the states of the four quarters? The poem “The Cuckoo” praises the goodness of the gentleman’s intentions. We may imagine the meaning conveyed through its evocative imagery as follows: The heart is the source of all transformation, and one’s person is the standard for the four quarters. Here I am moved by the gentleman. That cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, while its young are in the thorn tree: it does not, on account of its young, alter the constancy of its dwelling place. Even among other creatures this is so; how much more so with our good man, the gentleman! Grounded in a heart as firmly bound as a knot, he has established the substance beyond the great bounds [?]; manifested outwardly as a constant standard, it naturally accords with an appearance of balance and rectitude. Expressed through his four limbs, it is not merely that his deportment is consistent: bringing ritual propriety to bear in order to…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
治躬者則淑慎而不愆焉殆秩然於規矩之中
者乎見之一身不惟其帶弁然也率履之不越
者又俾臧而俾嘉焉殆儼然於瞻視之表者乎
夫其儀不忒如此吾知道範既端而彰之軌物
自足以動丕式之衷表儀克正則樹之風聲自
足以廣維新之化仰維德之隅而非僻之念可
潛消焉君子雖不期於心法之昭而四國羣然
其革心矣蜉蝣之習不於此而丕變耶覩令望
之孚而匪彝之從可默奪焉君子固無意於身
===
法之立而四國翕然其向風矣亦芾之偕不於
此而改觀耶是可見正乎己者即所以正乎人
而欲方外者尤不可不直乎內也噫君子其賢
乎考之召公告成王曰令聞令望四方之綱抑
之自戒曰敬慎威儀維民之則蓋威儀所以定
命而民之具瞻係焉鳲鳩詩人之言固有所本
也說者以為此詩指僖負羈而言嗚呼曹之赤
芾乘軒者三百人以斯人而不用何以望四國
之正也有正人之責者尚鑒茲哉
punctuated: 治躬者，則淑慎而不愆焉，殆秩然於規矩之中者乎！見之一身，不惟其帶弁然也，率履之不越者，又俾臧而俾嘉焉，殆儼然於瞻視之表者乎！夫其儀不忒如此，吾知道範既端，而彰之軌物，自足以動丕式之衷；表儀克正，則樹之風聲，自足以廣維新之化。仰維德之隅，而非僻之念可潛消焉，君子雖不期於心法之昭，而四國羣然其革心矣，蜉蝣之習不於此而丕變耶？覩令望之孚，而匪彝之從可默奪焉，君子固無意於身法之立，而四國翕然其向風矣，亦芾之偕不於此而改觀耶？是可見正乎己者，即所以正乎人，而欲方外者，尤不可不直乎內也。噫！君子其賢乎！考之召公告成王曰：「令聞令望，四方之綱。」《抑》之自戒曰：「敬慎威儀，維民之則。」蓋威儀所以定命，而民之具瞻係焉。鳲鳩詩人之言，固有所本也。說者以為此詩指僖負羈而言。嗚呼！曹之赤芾乘軒者三百人，以斯人而不用，何以望四國之正也？有正人之責者，尚鑒茲哉！
translation_en:
…in governing his own person, he is good and circumspect, committing no fault. Is he not orderly within the bounds of established standards? As manifested in his person, it is not merely his sash and cap that are proper: by following the prescribed course without overstepping it, he makes his conduct both good and admirable. Does he not present a dignified example for all to behold?

Since his deportment is thus without error, I know that, once his exemplary adherence to the Way is upright, the standards he makes manifest will themselves suffice to stir people’s hearts to take him as their great model. Once his exemplary bearing is correct, the moral influence he establishes will itself suffice to extend the transforming work of renewal. Looking up to the distinct outlines of his virtue, people may find their deviant thoughts imperceptibly dissolved. Although the gentleman does not seek to make manifest a model for the mind, the people of the four quarters will together reform their hearts. Will the habits depicted in “The Mayfly” not thereby be greatly changed? Beholding the trust inspired by his fine reputation, people may silently be turned away from following what violates constant moral norms. Although the gentleman has no intention of establishing his person as a model, the people of the four quarters will unanimously turn toward his influence. Will the company of those wearing red knee-covers [?] not thereby take on a different appearance?

From this we can see that rectifying oneself is precisely the means of rectifying others; and one who wishes to be square in outward conduct must, above all, be straight within. Ah, how worthy the gentleman is! Consider what the Duke of Shao told King Cheng: “A good name and a fine reputation are the guiding cords of the four quarters.” The self-admonition in “Restraint” says: “Be reverent and cautious in your dignified bearing, for it is the people’s model.” Dignified bearing is indeed what secures one’s allotted destiny, and upon it depends the gaze of all the people. The words of the poet of “The Cuckoo” thus certainly have a foundation.

Commentators hold that this poem refers to Xi Fuji. Alas! In Cao there were three hundred men who wore red knee-covers and rode in high carriages. If a man such as this was left unused, how could one hope for the rectification of the four quarters? May those responsible for rectifying others take warning from this!

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
思皇多士生此王國王國克生維周之楨
文在中〔王國寔作盛世天下維楨多〕〔丞汲下〕
同考試官教諭李　批〔以□□句詠歎本旨是篇獨就周邦言且發揮維楨切當明健允邁多士可錄〕
考試官教諭張　批〔贍整醇雅善作雅義者〕
考試官學正高　批〔和平流亮〕
詩人美周室之多賢而有輔國之忠焉夫賢才
之生以爲國也有周人才之盛則其爲國之楨
也固其所哉周公述天之福文王此自其臣庶
===
言之也蓋曰我周之興翊之者賢也生之者天
也周士傳世之顯豈偶然哉蓋美哉此多士也
勉敬之猶有以發至治之精華而乘時以出咸
萃于聖作之時勵翼之謨有以昭文德之宣朗
而應運以生畢集于周邦之內貞元會而豪傑
興一時師師之彥殆匹休乎唐虞之盛矣氣化
隆而賢哲奮一代藹藹之英誠遠邁乎夏商之
世矣夫以王國而能生此多士如此豈不有益
於國哉吾見秉精白以承休所以顯其經綸之
punctuated:
「思皇多士，生此王國。王國克生，維周之楨。」
文在中〔王國寔作盛世天下維楨多〕〔丞汲下〕
同考試官教諭李　批〔以□□句詠歎本旨，是篇獨就周邦言，且發揮維楨切當，明健允邁，多士可錄。〕
考試官教諭張　批〔贍整醇雅，善作雅義者。〕
考試官學正高　批〔和平流亮。〕
詩人美周室之多賢，而有輔國之忠焉。夫賢才之生，以爲國也。有周人才之盛，則其爲國之楨也，固其所哉！周公述天之福文王，此自其臣庶言之也。蓋曰：我周之興，翊之者賢也，生之者天也。周士傳世之顯，豈偶然哉？蓋美哉，此多士也！勉敬之猶，有以發至治之精華，而乘時以出，咸萃于聖作之時；勵翼之謨，有以昭文德之宣朗，而應運以生，畢集于周邦之內。貞元會而豪傑興，一時師師之彥，殆匹休乎唐虞之盛矣；氣化隆而賢哲奮，一代藹藹之英，誠遠邁乎夏商之世矣。夫以王國而能生此多士如此，豈不有益於國哉？吾見秉精白以承休，所以顯其經綸之
translation_en:
“How splendid are the many worthy men, born in this royal kingdom! The royal kingdom can indeed bring them forth: they are the pillars of Zhou.”
Wen Zaizhong 文在中. 〔“The royal kingdom indeed creates a flourishing age; all under Heaven … many pillars” [?; annotation garbled].〕〔“Assistant magistrate; Jixia” [?].〕
Associate Examiner Li, an Instructor, comments: 〔“The lines □□ express the central meaning through praise and exclamation. This essay speaks specifically of the realm of Zhou, and its exposition of ‘the pillars’ is apt. Clear and vigorous, it is truly outstanding; among the many candidates, its author merits selection.”〕
Examiner Zhang, an Instructor, comments: 〔“Ample and orderly, pure and elegant: one skilled in expounding the meaning of the Odes of the Kingdom.”〕
Examiner Gao, a School Instructor, comments: 〔“Balanced and mild, fluent and clear.”〕
The poet praises the Zhou royal house for its many worthy men, who possess the loyalty needed to support the state. Worthy and talented men are born to serve their country. With talent flourishing so abundantly under Zhou, was it not fitting that these men should become the pillars of the state? The Duke of Zhou recounts how Heaven blessed King Wen, speaking here in terms of his ministers and subjects. It is as though he says: “In the rise of our Zhou, it was worthy men who lent their support, and Heaven that brought them forth. Could the distinction of Zhou’s gentlemen, continuing from generation to generation, have been merely accidental?”
How admirable were these many worthy men! Their counsels of diligence and reverence brought forth the finest qualities of perfect government. Coming forward at the opportune moment, they all assembled when the sage arose. Their plans for diligent assistance manifested the radiance of civil virtue. Born in response to the destined age, they gathered within the realm of Zhou. As the cosmic cycle passed from completion to renewal, exceptional men arose; the worthies of that time, emulating one another, nearly equaled the glory of the flourishing age of Tang and Yu. As the transforming vital forces reached their height, worthy and wise men bestirred themselves; the multitude of eminent men of that generation truly far surpassed those of the Xia and Shang eras.
Since the royal kingdom could bring forth so many worthy men of this kind, how could they fail to benefit the state? I see them upholding purity of purpose to receive Heaven’s favor, thereby displaying their capacity to order affairs …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
禦者自足以成夫保障之功殫忠貞以自效所
以弘其賛相之能者自足以建夫屏翰之績自
其德之所培植也扶國運而繫人心有以鞏皇
圖于有永我周植本之固孰非其夾輔之力哉
自其才之所樹立也保人民而安社稷有以奠
國祚于無疆我周郟鄏之鼎孰非其底定之勳
哉夫以王國克生乎多士固足以見天厚有周
之意多士能忠乎國家又可以見多士承天之
心則其傳世之顯也宜哉雖然周士之生固本
===
于天而文王菁莪棫樸之化所以涵濡之者久
矣其始也純德以作人其終也任賢以佐命此
文德之所以盛而天命所由歸也周公欲成王
法祖以用賢而拳拳于周士傳世之顯及召公
卷阿之詠又以得賢自輔終之老成之告君類
若此厥后成王爲有周令主者周召之功偉矣
春秋
春王正月公會齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯
許男曹伯侵蔡蔡潰遂伐楚次于陘
punctuated:
禦者，自足以成夫保障之功；殫忠貞以自效，所以弘其賛相之能者，自足以建夫屏翰之績。自其德之所培植也，扶國運而繫人心，有以鞏皇圖于有永。我周植本之固，孰非其夾輔之力哉？自其才之所樹立也，保人民而安社稷，有以奠國祚于無疆。我周郟鄏之鼎，孰非其底定之勳哉？夫以王國克生乎多士，固足以見天厚有周之意；多士能忠乎國家，又可以見多士承天之心。則其傳世之顯也，宜哉！雖然，周士之生固本于天，而文王菁莪棫樸之化，所以涵濡之者久矣。其始也，純德以作人；其終也，任賢以佐命。此文德之所以盛，而天命所由歸也。周公欲成王法祖以用賢，而拳拳于周士傳世之顯；及召公卷阿之詠，又以得賢自輔終之。老成之告君，類若此。厥后成王爲有周令主者，周召之功偉矣！
春秋
春，王正月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯侵蔡，蔡潰，遂伐楚，次于陘。
translation_en:
…those who exercise governance [?] are themselves fully capable of safeguarding the state. Those who devote all their loyalty and steadfastness to its service, thereby extending their capacity to assist the ruler, are themselves fully capable of achieving distinction as its bulwarks. Through what their virtue nurtures, they sustain the fortunes of the state and bind the people’s hearts to it, securing the imperial enterprise forever. How could the firm foundations of our Zhou be anything other than the result of their supporting efforts? Through what their talents establish, they protect the people and bring peace to the altars of soil and grain, securing the dynasty’s fortunes without limit. How could the stability of our Zhou’s tripods at Jiaru be anything other than the achievement of their work of pacification? That the royal realm could bring forth so many worthy men certainly reveals Heaven’s intention to favor Zhou generously; that these men could serve the state loyally also reveals their resolve to fulfill Heaven’s will. It is thus fitting that they should remain illustrious through successive generations!
Nevertheless, although the emergence of Zhou’s worthy men ultimately originated in Heaven, King Wen’s transforming influence, celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood” (Jing E) and “The Oak and the Shrub” (Yu Pu), had long nurtured them. At the outset, he cultivated men through pure virtue; in the end, he employed the worthy to assist in fulfilling the heavenly mandate. This explains the flourishing of his civil virtue and why Heaven’s mandate came to him. The Duke of Zhou wished King Cheng to emulate his ancestor in employing the worthy, and therefore dwelt earnestly upon the enduring eminence of Zhou’s men. Likewise, the Duke of Shao’s poem “The Winding Mound” (Juan A) concluded with obtaining worthy men to assist the ruler. Such was the counsel these seasoned elders offered their sovereign. That King Cheng subsequently became an excellent ruler of Zhou owed much to the great achievements of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao!
Spring and Autumn Annals
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
楚屈完來盟于師盟于召陵〔俱僖公四年〕
冬公會晉侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾
子滕子薛伯杞伯小邾子齊世子光伐
鄭十有二月己亥同盟于戲〔襄公九年〕
周策
同考試官教諭孟　批〔塲中作者類多勦說此作於桓悼服楚心事義正詞嚴是有自得之學者錄之以式多士〕
考試官教諭張　批〔謹嚴得體〕
考試官學正高　批〔純正可誦〕
===
春秋於二霸兵好而皆美其得善勝之道焉此
桓之服楚悼之敵楚皆不戰而屈人兵者也其
斯以爲善之善者與夫自聃伯見俘孔叔勤德
八國之衆所爲集於陘也維時奇兵掠境而蔡
潰正兵聲罪而楚恐齊之兵力亦章章乎其無
敵矣使驕暴者處此鮮不動其好勝之念方城
漢水之險安能保其必克乎所幸節制之師仲
父素定而桓也任之脩文告以威敵而用之有
punctuated:
楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵。〔俱僖公四年〕
冬，公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子、齊世子光伐鄭。十有二月己亥，同盟于戲。〔襄公九年〕
周策
同考試官教諭孟批〔塲中作者類多勦說，此作於桓悼服楚心事，義正詞嚴，是有自得之學者，錄之以式多士。〕
考試官教諭張批〔謹嚴得體。〕
考試官學正高批〔純正可誦。〕
春秋於二霸兵好，而皆美其得善勝之道焉。此桓之服楚，悼之敵楚，皆不戰而屈人兵者也。其斯以爲善之善者與！夫自聃伯見俘，孔叔勤德，八國之衆所爲集於陘也。維時奇兵掠境而蔡潰，正兵聲罪而楚恐，齊之兵力亦章章乎其無敵矣。使驕暴者處此，鮮不動其好勝之念。方城漢水之險，安能保其必克乎？所幸節制之師，仲父素定，而桓也任之，脩文告以威敵，而用之有
translation_en:
…Qu Wan of Chu came to the army to conclude a covenant; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling. 〔Both passages concern the fourth year of Duke Xi.〕
In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Lesser Zhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the jihai day, they jointly entered into a covenant at Xi. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xiang.〕
Zhou Ce
Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor, comments: 〔Most writers in the examination compound borrow others’ explanations. This composition treats the intentions and actions of Dukes Huan and Dao in bringing Chu into submission with correct principles and rigorous language. Its author possesses learning gained through his own understanding. It is recorded here as a model for the candidates.〕
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Careful, rigorous, and appropriate in form.〕
Examiner Gao, School Director, comments: 〔Pure and correct; worthy of recitation.〕
The Spring and Autumn Annals, in treating the military and diplomatic dealings [?] of the two hegemons, praises both for attaining the way of achieving victory well. Duke Huan’s subjugation of Chu and Duke Dao’s opposition to Chu both subdued another’s forces without battle. Might these not be considered the highest excellence?
Now, following Dan Bo’s capture and Kong Shu’s exhortation to cultivate virtue, the forces of eight states assembled at Xing for this purpose. At that time, a surprise force raided the frontier and Cai collapsed; the main force proclaimed Chu’s offenses and Chu became afraid. The invincibility of Qi’s military strength was manifest indeed. Had an arrogant and violent man occupied this position, he could scarcely have avoided being stirred by a craving for victory. Yet, faced with the formidable defenses of Fangcheng and the Han River, how could he have guaranteed conquest?
Fortunately, Zhongfu had long established a disciplined army, and Duke Huan entrusted matters to him. He prepared formal proclamations to overawe the enemy, and employed his forces with…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
律亟退舍以結盟而下之有禮雖不必戰勝攻
取而徼好承顧楚巳帖然服矣不謂之善勝可
乎春秋取其近王事也是故美召陵焉畏謀不
從騑任其咎三駕之役所爲講於戲也維時鄭
待二境以請盟楚肆北圖而力競晉之伯業亦
落落乎其難合矣使忿疾者處此將不勝其求
逞之心荆尸兩廣之雄安能保其必捷乎所幸
善陣之法武子能明而悼也聽之分軍逆來而
於我未病還師許盟而彼不能從雖不必暴骨
===
以爭而大勞未艾楚巳索然屈矣不謂之善勝
可乎春秋取其能駕外也是故下書蕭魚以美
焉凡此皆愼用兵重民命而惡以兵刃相接聖
人之情見巳惜乎召陵之後濤塗執陳見侵桓
志巳盈蕭魚之續偉矣釁啓通吳政委大夫事
日非焉不然以桓公正而不譎晉悼君子之資
幾何而不進於王德哉此管仲知罃所以終於
伯佐而巳噫覯文匿武之訓顧取威定霸者所
能久假耶
punctuated:
律，亟退舍以結盟，而下之有禮。雖不必戰勝攻取，而徼好承顧，楚巳帖然服矣。不謂之善勝可乎？春秋取其近王事也，是故美召陵焉。畏謀不從，騑任其咎，三駕之役所爲講於戲也。維時鄭待二境以請盟，楚肆北圖而力競，晉之伯業亦落落乎其難合矣。使忿疾者處此，將不勝其求逞之心，荆尸兩廣之雄，安能保其必捷乎？所幸善陣之法，武子能明，而悼也聽之。分軍逆來，而於我未病；還師許盟，而彼不能從。雖不必暴骨以爭，而大勞未艾，楚巳索然屈矣。不謂之善勝可乎？春秋取其能駕外也，是故下書蕭魚以美焉。
凡此皆愼用兵、重民命，而惡以兵刃相接，聖人之情見巳。惜乎召陵之後，濤塗執，陳見侵，桓志巳盈；蕭魚之續，偉矣釁啓，通吳，政委大夫，事日非焉。不然，以桓公正而不譎、晉悼君子之資，幾何而不進於王德哉？此管仲、知罃所以終於伯佐而巳。噫！覯文匿武之訓，顧取威定霸者所能久假耶？
translation_en:
…discipline; he promptly withdrew his forces to conclude a covenant, treating the other side with ritual courtesy in his condescension. Without necessarily winning battles or capturing territory, he sought friendly relations and received favorable regard [?], and Chu had already submitted meekly. Can this fail to be called skill in victory? The Spring and Autumn Annals approves of his approaching the deeds of a true king, and therefore praises the covenant at Shaoling.
The plan prompted by fear was not followed, and Fei bore the blame [?]; the operations of the three successive mobilizations were discussed at Xi. At that time, Zheng waited for the two powers to reach its borders before requesting a covenant, while Chu pursued its designs in the north and competed vigorously. Jin’s hegemonic enterprise was thus far from readily securing unity. Had an angry and impetuous man occupied this position, he would have been unable to restrain his desire to prevail. Against the might of Chu’s battle formations and its two divisions of chariots, how could he have guaranteed victory? Fortunately, Wuzi understood the methods of effective military deployment, and Duke Dao listened to him. He divided the armies to meet the enemy’s advance, leaving his own side unexhausted; he withdrew his forces and allowed a covenant, while the enemy could not keep up. Without necessarily fighting until bones lay exposed, he kept Chu’s severe exertions unremitting, and Chu had already yielded in exhaustion. Can this fail to be called skill in victory? The Spring and Autumn Annals approves of his ability to control the outer states; therefore, in the subsequent entry, it records Xiaoyu to praise him.
All these instances show caution in employing troops, regard for the people’s lives, and aversion to clashes of weapons: the Sage’s sentiments are manifest. Regrettably, after Shaoling, Taotu was arrested and Chen suffered invasion: Duke Huan’s ambitions had already become overweening. In the aftermath of Xiaoyu, troubles arose amid great achievements [?]; relations were established with Wu, government was entrusted to the grandees, and affairs deteriorated daily. Otherwise, given Duke Huan’s uprightness and freedom from deceit, and Duke Dao of Jin’s qualities as a gentleman, how far could they have been from advancing to kingly virtue? This is why Guan Zhong and Zhi Ying ultimately remained merely assistants to hegemons. Alas! Could those intent on acquiring intimidating power and establishing hegemony long sustain even a borrowed adherence to the injunction to display civil virtue and conceal martial force [?]?

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
公會晉侯及吳子于黃池哀公十有三年
邊自化
同考試官教諭孟　批〔聖人治御之意見諸書法此作〕
發明透徹謹嚴莊重誦之令人斂衽三嘆傑士也高薦允宜
考試官教諭張　批〔識見迥別是深於春秋者〕
考試官學正高　批〔簡切有味〕
春秋紀兩伯之會而嚴其詞所以示治內御外
之道也夫兩伯自黃池始也先晉子吳而言及
聖人於夷夏盛衰之際其嚴乎且貴華賤夷而
===
冠屨之分正扶陽抑陰而天地之義明斯則春
秋傾否之書聖人經世之略其謹嚴固如是也
晉定失霸夫差暴橫託伯父之尊屬襲僭王之
餘威黃池會而侈然肆其雄長之爭魯衛同而
儼然厭於宗盟之上岌岌乎內外潰決而經常
倒置矣經斯世者寧弗加之意耶是故吳固主
會序晉爲先蓋盟主之常尊非僭夷之所得加
也春秋內中國而外諸夷不以是夫吳已稱王
正名爲子蓋一人之大號非命圭之所可假也
punctuated:
公會晉侯及吳子于黃池。哀公十有三年。
邊自化
同考試官教諭孟批〔聖人治御之意見諸書法，此作〕發明透徹，謹嚴莊重，誦之令人斂衽三嘆，傑士也，高薦允宜。
考試官教諭張批〔識見迥別，是深於春秋者。〕
考試官學正高批〔簡切有味。〕
春秋紀兩伯之會而嚴其詞，所以示治內御外之道也。夫兩伯自黃池始也，先晉、子吳而言及，聖人於夷夏盛衰之際，其嚴乎！且貴華賤夷而冠屨之分正，扶陽抑陰而天地之義明，斯則春秋傾否之書、聖人經世之略，其謹嚴固如是也。晉定失霸，夫差暴橫，託伯父之尊屬，襲僭王之餘威。黃池會而侈然肆其雄長之爭，魯衛同而儼然厭於宗盟之上，岌岌乎內外潰決而經常倒置矣！經斯世者，寧弗加之意耶？是故吳固主會，序晉爲先，蓋盟主之常尊，非僭夷之所得加也。春秋內中國而外諸夷，不以是夫？吳已稱王，正名爲子，蓋一人之大號，非命圭之所可假也。
translation_en:
“The duke met with the Marquis of Jin and the Viscount of Wu at Huangchi.” Thirteenth year of Duke Ai.

Bian Zihua

Comment by Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor: 〔The Sage’s intention in governing the interior and controlling the exterior appears in his manner of recording events. This composition〕 elucidates it thoroughly and lucidly. Meticulous, rigorous, dignified, and solemn, it makes the reader straighten his robes in reverence and sigh repeatedly in admiration. An outstanding scholar! His recommendation for a high placing is entirely fitting.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔His insight is exceptionally discerning: here is someone deeply versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals.〕

Comment by Examiner Gao, School Instructor: 〔Concise and incisive, with much to savor.〕

The Spring and Autumn Annals records the meeting of two hegemons with exacting language, thereby revealing the way to govern the interior and control the exterior. The coexistence of two hegemons began at Huangchi. By placing Jin first, calling Wu a viscount, and using the conjunction “and,” how exacting the Sage was at this juncture in the waxing and waning of the foreign peoples and the Chinese! Furthermore, by honoring the Chinese and lowering the foreign peoples, he set right the distinction between cap and shoes; by supporting yang and restraining yin, he clarified the proper relations of Heaven and Earth. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book for overturning obstruction, and embodies the Sage’s plan for ordering the world. Such, indeed, is its meticulous rigor.

Duke Ding of Jin had lost the hegemony, while Fuchai was violent and overbearing. Relying on the honored kinship designation “senior paternal uncle,” and drawing on the residual awe of his usurped royal title, he met the others at Huangchi and arrogantly pressed his contest for supremacy. With Lu and Wei also present, he presumptuously dominated the assembly of the covenanting clans. How perilous it was: the boundaries between interior and exterior were collapsing, and the enduring norms were being overturned! Could one who sought to order such an age fail to attend to this?

Therefore, although Wu in fact presided over the meeting, Jin is placed first in the record. For the established dignity of the covenant leader could not be superseded by a usurping foreign ruler. Is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals treats the Central States as the interior and the various foreign peoples as the exterior? Wu had already assumed the title of king, but the text rectifies his designation by calling him a viscount. For the exalted title belonging to the One Man could not be borrowed by one invested with a jade tablet of enfeoffment.

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
春秋四夷雖大皆曰子不以是夫然晉雖居前
吳實並霸先吳不免於拂經列書尤嫌於泯實
特書曰及而天地之大經以順會盟之霸迹足
徵使吳不得自遂其强晉不至終底於弱聖人
立法垂訓之嚴如此夫然後防立而中國有常
勝焉名正而四夷有定守焉要無事乎持衡爭
長大經一順而抑鋒止銳亦自有餘策矣後世
乃有顛倒冠屨以有天下者將欲保國而免其
侵暴得乎噫由不講於治內御外之道故耳撥
===
亂世反之正非聖人其孰能之雖然聖人之不
得已也使中國猶有人焉蕞爾夷吳猶不能拒
於越之入何至主盟上國哉乃魯甘百牢之徵
衛懼國狗之瘈非獨晉俛首東向而聽命也若
夫持節旄以尊漢爭獻納以伸宋者其亦聞黃
池之訓而興起者與
禮記
天子者與天地參故德配天地兼利萬物
與日月並明明照四海而不遺微小其
punctuated:
春秋四夷雖大皆曰子，不以是夫？然晉雖居前，吳實並霸，先吳不免於拂經，列書尤嫌於泯實。特書曰「及」，而天地之大經以順，會盟之霸迹足徵，使吳不得自遂其强，晉不至終底於弱。聖人立法垂訓之嚴如此夫！然後防立而中國有常勝焉，名正而四夷有定守焉。要無事乎持衡爭長，大經一順，而抑鋒止銳亦自有餘策矣。後世乃有顛倒冠屨以有天下者，將欲保國而免其侵暴，得乎？噫！由不講於治內御外之道故耳。撥亂世反之正，非聖人其孰能之？雖然，聖人之不得已也。使中國猶有人焉，蕞爾夷吳猶不能拒於越之入，何至主盟上國哉？乃魯甘百牢之徵，衛懼國狗之瘈，非獨晉俛首東向而聽命也。若夫持節旄以尊漢，爭獻納以伸宋者，其亦聞黃池之訓而興起者與？

禮記

天子者，與天地參，故德配天地，兼利萬物，與日月並明，明照四海而不遺微小。其
translation_en:
…Is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals calls the rulers of all the outer peoples “viscount” (zi), however great their states? Yet although Jin was placed first, Wu in fact shared the hegemony. Placing Wu first would inevitably violate the canonical norm, while merely listing them would risk obscuring the facts. The deliberate use of the word “and” thus upheld the great ordering principle of Heaven and Earth while leaving verifiable evidence of the hegemons’ conduct at the covenant assembly. It prevented Wu from freely asserting its strength and Jin from sinking irretrievably into weakness. Such was the rigor with which the Sage established rules and transmitted instruction! Only then were boundaries established, giving the central states enduring ascendancy; names were rectified, giving the outer peoples fixed limits to observe. Ultimately, there was no need to balance power and compete for precedence. Once the great ordering principle was upheld, ample means would naturally remain to curb aggression and check its advance. Yet in later ages there were those who possessed All under Heaven while turning the proper order upside down, placing shoes above caps. Could they hope to preserve their states and escape violent encroachment? Alas! This arose simply from failing to study the way to govern within and resist threats from without. Who but the Sage could bring an age of disorder back to rectitude? Even so, the Sage acted only because he had no alternative. Had the central states still possessed capable men, how could the petty outer state of Wu, unable even to repel an invasion by Yuyue, have come to preside over a covenant among the central states? Yet Lu submitted willingly to the levy of a hundred sets of sacrificial animals, and Wei feared the frenzy of the state’s rabid dogs [?]. It was not Jin alone that bowed its head, faced east, and obeyed commands. As for those who upheld their yak-tail-tufted credentials to honor Han, or contended over the presentation of offerings to uphold Song [?], were they too inspired to action by hearing the lesson of Huangchi?

Book of Rites

The Son of Heaven forms a triad with Heaven and Earth. Thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, benefiting all things alike; his brightness equals that of the sun and moon, illuminating the Four Seas without neglecting even the smallest things. His…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
在朝廷則道仁聖禮義之序燕處則□
雅頌之音行步則有環佩之聲升車則
有鸞和之音居處有禮進退有度百官
得其宜萬事得其序
閻應儒
同考試官教諭粟　批　〔此題草作者不難於措詞而難於體認聖人立言之意此篇有甚酌有含蓄具於序宜處即以仁聖禮義發揮〕〔□□得經旨足錄式〕
考試官教諭張　批　發養處明確可誦而忌愛之意
溢於言表取之
===
考試官學正高　批　〔并通得體〕
記者贊君德之極盛必言其養之純而及其驗
也夫德侔造化不易致也苟非隨寓而純其所
養之功焉又何以獲其驗乎記者之意若曰德
之未盛者不足以同天養之未純者不足以昭
德惟天子得天之厚而爲民之主也吾見其道
參天地而兩儀之克配者有以兼濟萬物而無
外道何大也明並日明而四表之光被者有以
旁燭微小而不遺德何明也夫天子道德之盛
punctuated:
在朝廷，則道仁聖禮義之序；燕處，則□雅頌之音；行步，則有環佩之聲；升車，則有鸞和之音。居處有禮，進退有度，百官得其宜，萬事得其序。
閻應儒
同考試官教諭粟批：〔此題草作者不難於措詞，而難於體認聖人立言之意。此篇有甚酌，有含蓄，具於序宜處，即以仁聖禮義發揮〕〔□□得經旨，足錄式〕

考試官學正高批：〔并通得體〕
記者贊君德之極盛，必言其養之純而及其驗也。夫德侔造化，不易致也。苟非隨寓而純其所養之功焉，又何以獲其驗乎？記者之意若曰：德之未盛者，不足以同天；養之未純者，不足以昭德。惟天子得天之厚，而爲民之主也。吾見其道參天地，而兩儀之克配者，有以兼濟萬物而無外，道何大也！明並日明，而四表之光被者，有以旁燭微小而不遺，德何明也！夫天子道德之盛
translation_en:
…At court, he speaks of the proper ordering of benevolence, sageliness, ritual propriety, and righteousness; in private repose, he [illegible character] the sounds of the Odes and Hymns. When he walks, his jade pendants sound; when he mounts his carriage, its luan and he bells sound. His daily conduct accords with ritual propriety, and his advances and withdrawals have due measure. The hundred officials each find their proper place, and the myriad affairs attain their proper order.

Yan Yingru.

Comment by Associate Examiner Su, Instructor: 〔For those composing on this topic, the difficulty lies not in phrasing but in apprehending the sage’s intention in making this statement. This essay shows deliberation [?] and restraint. In its treatment of “order” and “proper place,” it develops the meaning through benevolence, sageliness, ritual propriety, and righteousness.〕〔[Two illegible characters] grasps the purport of the classic and merits inclusion as a model.〕

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: Its exposition of cultivation is clear and worthy of recitation, while its sense of aversion and affection [?] overflows beyond the words. Accept it.

Comment by Examiner Gao, Instructor: 〔Coherent throughout and appropriate in form.〕

When the recorder praises the supreme flourishing of the ruler’s virtue, he necessarily speaks of the purity of its cultivation and proceeds to its manifestations. To make one’s virtue equal to the transforming work of Heaven and Earth is no easy achievement. Unless one perfects the work of cultivation in every circumstance, how can one obtain its manifestations? The recorder’s meaning is as if to say: virtue that has not flourished fully cannot equal Heaven; cultivation that has not become pure cannot make virtue manifest. It is the Son of Heaven who receives Heaven’s abundant endowment and becomes the people’s lord. I see that his Way stands alongside Heaven and Earth: his ability to match these two powers enables him to benefit all things, excluding none. How great is his Way! His brightness equals “the sun’s brightness” [?]; its radiance reaches the four outermost bounds, enabling him to illuminate even the smallest things on every side, overlooking none. How luminous is his virtue! Now, the flourishing of the Son of Heaven’s Way and virtue…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
如此然豈自治之疎者所能致哉蓋無適而不
得其養者矣是故其在朝廷則仁聖迭運也禮
義時出也而所由不紊其序豈非備道於大觀
之地乎其在燕居則二雅必奏也三頌必陳也
而所聽不濫其音何嘗自肆於幽獨之地乎不
寧惟是其致樂以治心者雖行步升車不廢焉
而環佩鑾和相繼也其致禮以治躬者於居處
進退必謹焉而有禮有度不爽也如是而豈無
效之可言耶但見元首明而股肱爲之自良大
===
臣法而小臣廉也百官於是乎宜矣是宜者義
也而天子道義之效不可徵乎股肱良而庶事
爲之自康大綱舉而衆目張也萬事於是乎序
矣是序者禮也而天子道禮之效不可徵乎合
是而爲樂之和爲仁聖之用日月同明天地同
德由此其致矣天子之德一何盛哉抑考古之
帝王盛德大業未有不先於治已之功者故無
怠荒而克勤儉虞夏所以得天也制事制心敬
勝義勝商周所以受命也故古之大臣所以告
punctuated: 如此，然豈自治之疎者所能致哉？蓋無適而不得其養者矣。是故其在朝廷，則仁聖迭運也，禮義時出也，而所由不紊其序，豈非備道於大觀之地乎？其在燕居，則二雅必奏也，三頌必陳也，而所聽不濫其音，何嘗自肆於幽獨之地乎？不寧惟是，其致樂以治心者，雖行步升車不廢焉，而環佩鑾和相繼也；其致禮以治躬者，於居處進退必謹焉，而有禮有度不爽也。如是而豈無效之可言耶？但見元首明而股肱爲之自良，大臣法而小臣廉也，百官於是乎宜矣。是宜者，義也，而天子道義之效不可徵乎？股肱良而庶事爲之自康，大綱舉而衆目張也，萬事於是乎序矣。是序者，禮也，而天子道禮之效不可徵乎？合是而爲樂之和，爲仁聖之用，日月同明，天地同德，由此其致矣。天子之德一何盛哉！抑考古之帝王，盛德大業，未有不先於治已之功者。故無怠荒而克勤儉，虞夏所以得天也；制事制心，敬勝義勝，商周所以受命也。故古之大臣所以告
translation_en:
…is such. Yet how could anyone lax in governing himself attain it? Surely, wherever he goes, he receives the nourishment needed for his cultivation. Thus, at court, benevolence and sagely wisdom operate in turn, and ritual propriety and righteousness manifest themselves at the proper times. His conduct never disrupts their order: does he not thereby embody the Way fully in a place exposed to public view? In his private residence, the Lesser and Greater Odes are invariably performed, and the Hymns of the three dynasties invariably presented. The sounds he hears admit no indiscriminate admixture: when has he ever indulged himself in the privacy of solitude? Nor is this all. In employing music to govern his heart, he never dispenses with it even when walking or mounting his carriage: the sounds of his jade pendants and carriage bells follow one another. In employing ritual propriety to govern his person, he is invariably careful in his dwelling, his movements, his advances, and his withdrawals; his observance of propriety and measure never falters.

With conduct like this, could there be no effects to speak of? We see only that when the head is enlightened, the arms and legs naturally become worthy: the high ministers conform to proper standards, and the lesser ministers remain incorruptible. All officials thus act fittingly. Such fitness is righteousness: can the effects of the Son of Heaven’s Way and righteousness not be verified here? When the arms and legs are worthy, the many affairs of government naturally flourish. When the main cord of the net is lifted, all its meshes open; the myriad affairs thus fall into order. Such order is ritual propriety: can the effects of the Son of Heaven’s Way and ritual propriety not be verified here? Together these constitute the harmony of music and the functioning of benevolence and sagely wisdom. From these he comes to share the brightness of the sun and moon and the virtue of Heaven and Earth. How abundant is the Son of Heaven’s virtue!

Moreover, if we examine the emperors and kings of antiquity, none attained abundant virtue and great achievements without first undertaking the work of governing himself. Thus, freedom from indolence and neglect, together with diligence and frugality, was how Yu and Xia won Heaven’s favor. Regulating affairs and governing the heart, with reverence and righteousness prevailing, was how Shang and Zhou received the Mandate. Hence, the means by which the great ministers of antiquity admonished…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
戒其君者一則曰天難諶斯一則曰克享天心
誠以人君繼天而爲之子其精神與天通一無
間理固如是耳匪引天以懼之也然則有志於
參天配天之治者其尚愼所以脩身養德以無
忘記禮者之言哉
先勞而後祿不亦易祿乎
侯官家
同考試官教諭栗　批〔理明詞到深得人臣敬事後食之心錄之以式多士〕
===
考試官教諭張　批〔發明易祿字義甚許〕
考試官學正高　批〔理致精切國之忠臣稱於其臣敬事敬服〕
君子敬其事而後其食此祿之所以易也蓋儒
者之心知盡其職而不謀利者也故先勞而後
獲其祿之也不亦易乎儒行載孔子告哀公之
意若曰純臣行義以達道不爲干祿之私明君
儲祿以養賢專爲勸事之報自夫下臣爲利祿
而效忠其道寖薄矣所謂儒者之易祿者果何
punctuated:
戒其君者，一則曰：「天難諶斯。」一則曰：「克享天心。」誠以人君繼天而爲之子，其精神與天通一無間，理固如是耳，匪引天以懼之也。然則有志於參天配天之治者，其尚愼所以脩身養德，以無忘記禮者之言哉！

先勞而後祿，不亦易祿乎？

侯官家

同考試官教諭栗，批〔理明詞到，深得人臣敬事後食之心，錄之以式多士。〕

考試官教諭張，批〔發明易祿字義甚許。〕

考試官學正高，批〔理致精切，國之忠臣，稱於其臣敬事敬服。〕

君子敬其事而後其食，此祿之所以易也。蓋儒者之心，知盡其職而不謀利者也，故先勞而後獲，其祿之也不亦易乎？《儒行》載孔子告哀公之意，若曰：純臣行義以達道，不爲干祿之私；明君儲祿以養賢，專爲勸事之報。自夫下臣爲利祿而效忠，其道寖薄矣。所謂儒者之易祿者，果何
translation_en:
…in admonishing their rulers, some said, “Heaven is difficult to trust,” while others said, “Be capable of winning Heaven’s favor.” This is truly because the ruler succeeds Heaven and acts as its son: his spirit is united with Heaven without any separation. Such is the principle of things; these admonitions do not invoke Heaven merely to frighten him. Thus, those who aspire to a government that participates in Heaven’s work and matches its virtue should surely attend carefully to cultivating themselves and nurturing their virtue, never forgetting the words of those who recorded the rites!

“To labor first and receive emoluments afterward—is such a man not easy to remunerate?”

Hou Guanjia 侯官家

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔The reasoning is clear and the language apt. It profoundly captures the spirit of a minister who attends reverently to his duties and takes his sustenance afterward. Recorded here as a model for the assembled scholars.〕

Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Highly commendable for elucidating the meaning of “easy to remunerate.”〕

Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: 〔The reasoning is precise and incisive. A loyal minister of the state, praised among its ministers [?]; reverence for duty inspires reverent admiration [?].〕

The gentleman attends reverently to his duties and only afterward takes his sustenance: this is why he is easy to remunerate. The Confucian scholar’s mind is intent on fulfilling his office, without seeking personal profit. Thus he labors first and receives his reward afterward; is he not easy to remunerate? The chapter “The Conduct of the Confucian Scholar” records the substance of Confucius’s words to Duke Ai, as if to say: a minister of pure devotion practices righteousness to realize the Way, without any private ambition to obtain emoluments; an enlightened ruler sets aside emoluments to support worthy men, solely as recompense that encourages service. Once lesser ministers offer their loyalty for profit and emoluments, their moral commitment gradually declines. When it is said that the Confucian scholar is easy to remunerate, what, indeed, …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
所見乎彼人臣效力於君者謂勞也勞吾所當
自盡人君恤臣之私者有祿也祿吾不敢自必
故儒者之事君以義之不可逃也而力有所必
竭焉惟知勞於王事而志必先之以責之不可
諉也而心有所必殫焉是雖祿有常秩而意不
及之始焉不敢憚於勞也所以奮庸熙載者必
勑其初若夫祿以養廉惟君所命而已而未始
萌夫覬覦之私繼焉不敢倦於勞也所以圖成
代終者必虔其後若夫祿以代耕惟上所賜而
===
已而未始起夫期必之念夫如是不亦易祿乎
蓋其正誼而不謀利則廉靜之操本無厚望之
私先事而能後食則忠懇之懷不暇自營之計
雖祿以天下當與賢者共之然事專報主而祿
不入心不惟以功詔祿之易也即使代耕之食
不給焉亦勿恤矣豈曰得之難也而祿之不易
哉雖養賢之祿不爲儒者靳之然志存立功而
利不遑計不惟以事賁食之易也即使養廉之
具未周焉亦相忘矣豈曰畜之難也而祿之遂
punctuated: 所見乎？彼人臣效力於君者，謂勞也，勞吾所當自盡；人君恤臣之私者，有祿也，祿吾不敢自必。故儒者之事君，以義之不可逃也，而力有所必竭焉，惟知勞於王事，而志必先之；以責之不可諉也，而心有所必殫焉，是雖祿有常秩，而意不及之。始焉不敢憚於勞也，所以奮庸熙載者，必勑其初；若夫祿以養廉，惟君所命而已，而未始萌夫覬覦之私。繼焉不敢倦於勞也，所以圖成代終者，必虔其後；若夫祿以代耕，惟上所賜而已，而未始起夫期必之念。夫如是，不亦易祿乎？蓋其正誼而不謀利，則廉靜之操，本無厚望之私；先事而能後食，則忠懇之懷，不暇自營之計。雖祿以天下，當與賢者共之，然事專報主，而祿不入心，不惟以功詔祿之易也，即使代耕之食不給焉，亦勿恤矣，豈曰得之難也，而祿之不易哉？雖養賢之祿，不爲儒者靳之，然志存立功，而利不遑計，不惟以事賁食之易也，即使養廉之具未周焉，亦相忘矣，豈曰畜之難也，而祿之遂
translation_en:
…what understanding does this reveal? A subject’s exertions in his ruler’s service are called labor: in labor I ought to give my utmost. A ruler provides emoluments out of concern for his subjects’ personal needs: emoluments I dare not presume to receive. Thus, when a Confucian serves his ruler, he exhausts his strength because the demands of righteousness cannot be evaded. He knows only to labor in royal service, and sets his mind on this first. He devotes his whole heart because his responsibilities cannot be shifted to others. Although emoluments follow an established scale, his thoughts do not reach them. At the outset, he dares not shrink from labor: in exerting his abilities and bringing his duties to fruition, he must be diligent from the beginning. As for emoluments to sustain his integrity, these depend solely on the ruler’s command; no selfish desire to obtain them ever sprouts in his mind. Thereafter, he dares not grow weary of labor: in seeking accomplishment and carrying his charge through to completion, he must remain earnest to the end. As for emoluments in lieu of farming, these depend solely on what his sovereign bestows; he never entertains the thought that he must receive them. Is such a man not easy to remunerate?

He upholds righteousness without seeking profit; thus his incorruptible and tranquil disposition contains no selfish expectation of generous rewards. He puts service first and can leave remuneration until afterward; thus his loyal and earnest heart has no leisure to calculate his own advantage. Although the ruler enjoys the resources of the realm and ought to share them with the worthy, this man’s service is devoted solely to requiting his lord, and emoluments never enter his thoughts.
