title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
樊遲問仁子曰愛人問知子曰知人
文在中
同考試官教諭彭　批〔發明愛人知人精切渾融深得〕〔夫子語樊遲之意〕
考試官教諭張　批〔題本平易諸作鮮深淺獨此作詞簡義〕〔暢殊庶本旨取之以冠多士云〕
考試官學正高　批〔明順精確模寫夫子語氣宛然〕
===
雋士雋士
聖人因賢者志於仁知而教以善用其心焉蓋
德愛曰仁通曰知知人皆有是心也於此而知所
用焉仁知豈外是哉且道莫大於仁知夫固原
於一心而達之天下者也是故樊遲之在聖門
也以仁爲問焉夫子恐其近利之心易蔽以私
也乃告之曰仁主於愛而愛莫先於愛人其必
篤同類之誼而以恩相與務盡乎維持培植之
意擴民胞之度而以德相臨不失乎易直子諒
punctuated:
第壹場
四書
樊遲問仁，子曰：「愛人。」問知，子曰：「知人。」
文在中
同考試官教諭彭批〔發明愛人知人精切渾融深得〕〔夫子語樊遲之意〕
考試官教諭張批〔題本平易諸作鮮深淺獨此作詞簡義〕〔暢殊庶本旨取之以冠多士云〕
考試官學正高批〔明順精確模寫夫子語氣宛然〕
雋士雋士
聖人因賢者志於仁知，而教以善用其心焉。蓋德愛曰仁，通曰知，知人皆有是心也。於此而知所用焉，仁知豈外是哉？且道莫大於仁知，夫固原於一心而達之天下者也。是故樊遲之在聖門也，以仁爲問焉。夫子恐其近利之心易蔽以私也，乃告之曰：「仁主於愛，而愛莫先於愛人。其必篤同類之誼，而以恩相與，務盡乎維持培植之意；擴民胞之度，而以德相臨，不失乎易直子諒
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

Fan Chi asked about benevolence. The Master said, “Love others.” He asked about wisdom. The Master said, “Know others.”

Wen Zaizhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Instructor: “The exposition of loving others and knowing others is incisive, precise, and thoroughly integrated. It deeply grasps the Master's meaning in speaking to Fan Chi.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “The topic is fundamentally straightforward, yet few submissions distinguish depth from shallowness [?]. This composition alone is concise in expression and lucid in meaning, coming particularly close to the original purport. We have selected it to stand foremost among the candidates.”

Comment by Examiner Gao, School Director: “Clear, fluent, refined, and exact: it vividly reproduces the Master's manner of speaking.”

Outstanding scholar, outstanding scholar [?].

Because the worthy man aspired to benevolence and wisdom, the Sage taught him how to employ his heart well. For virtuous love is called benevolence, and understanding is called wisdom; in knowing others, all possess this heart [?]. If one knows how to employ it here, can benevolence and wisdom lie outside it? Moreover, nothing in the Way is greater than benevolence and wisdom. They surely originate in the single heart and extend throughout the world. Thus, when Fan Chi was studying in the Sage's school, he asked about benevolence. Fearing that his heart, inclined toward advantage, might easily be obscured by selfishness, the Master told him: “Benevolence rests principally upon love, and in love nothing takes precedence over loving others. One must strengthen the bonds with one's fellow human beings and deal with them graciously, striving fully to realize the intention of sustaining and nurturing them; one must broaden the generosity that regards the people as one's siblings and approach them with virtue, preserving an easy, upright, loving, and trustworthy …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
之衷一體以爲心也四海以爲家也而分之親
踈有不得而閒之焉是雖仁統萬善若不盡於
愛人卽此而天下之至公在我所謂唯仁人能
愛人者此也不謂之仁而何哉又以智爲問焉
夫子慮其麤鄙之心易淆其眞也乃告之曰智
主於知而知莫急於知人其必秉權度之精而
因言以考德務嚴夫淑慝之辨廣甄别之鑑而
緣迹以求心不爽乎是非之極以明覺則有常
也以品藻則不眩也而情之眞僞有不能以逃
之焉是雖知周萬物若不盡於知人卽此而天
下之至明在我所謂惟知者不失人此也不謂
之知而何哉要之愛人仁也非知人則無以成
其愛知人知也非愛人則無以行其知夫子一
言而盡天下之道矣惜乎樊遲不足以語此抑
考書曰知人則哲能官人安民則惠黎民懷之
夫子此言固帝王治天下之要道也豈止爲樊
遲荅問之教哉雖然不有子夏富哉之論則夫
子枉直之教將終晦矣昔人謂發聖人之蘊教
punctuated: 之衷，一體以爲心也，四海以爲家也，而分之親踈有不得而閒之焉。是雖仁統萬善，若不盡於愛人，卽此而天下之至公在我，所謂「唯仁人能愛人」者此也。不謂之仁而何哉？又以智爲問焉。夫子慮其麤鄙之心易淆其眞也，乃告之曰：「智主於知，而知莫急於知人。」其必秉權度之精，而因言以考德，務嚴夫淑慝之辨；廣甄别之鑑，而緣迹以求心，不爽乎是非之極。以明覺則有常也，以品藻則不眩也，而情之眞僞有不能以逃之焉。是雖知周萬物，若不盡於知人，卽此而天下之至明在我，所謂「惟知者不失人」此也。不謂之知而何哉？要之，愛人，仁也；非知人，則無以成其愛。知人，知也；非愛人，則無以行其知。夫子一言而盡天下之道矣。惜乎樊遲不足以語此！抑考《書》曰：「知人則哲，能官人；安民則惠，黎民懷之。」夫子此言，固帝王治天下之要道也，豈止爲樊遲荅問之教哉？雖然，不有子夏「富哉」之論，則夫子枉直之教將終晦矣。昔人謂：「發聖人之蘊，教
translation_en:
…the disposition of his heart. He takes all as one body in his concern and regards all within the Four Seas as his family; distinctions between close and distant relations cannot intrude to divide them. Although benevolence encompasses all goodness and would seem not to be exhausted by loving others, through this alone the utmost impartiality under Heaven resides in me. This is what is meant by “Only the benevolent person can love others.” If this is not called benevolence, what should it be called?
Fan Chi then also asked about wisdom. Confucius feared that the coarseness of his mind might readily obscure its genuine nature, and therefore told him: “Wisdom consists chiefly in knowing, and in knowing nothing is more urgent than knowing people.” One must hold precisely to the scales and measures of judgment, examining virtue through people’s words and rigorously distinguishing goodness from wickedness. One must broaden one’s discerning scrutiny, seeking people’s intentions through their actions without departing from the ultimate standard of right and wrong. In clear awareness one will thus be constant, and in appraising people one will not be confused; the sincerity or falsity of their dispositions cannot escape one. Although wisdom comprehends the myriad things and would seem not to be exhausted by knowing people, through this alone the utmost discernment under Heaven resides in me. This is what is meant by “Only the wise do not misjudge people.” If this is not called wisdom, what should it be called?
In essence, loving people is benevolence; without knowing people, one cannot bring that love to fulfillment. Knowing people is wisdom; without loving people, one cannot put that wisdom into practice. With a single utterance, Confucius encompassed the Way of all under Heaven. Alas, Fan Chi was not sufficiently advanced to be spoken to of this! Moreover, consider what the Book of Documents says: “Knowing people makes one wise, able to appoint people to office; bringing peace to the people makes one kind, and the common people cherish him.” These words of Confucius are indeed the essential Way by which emperors and kings govern all under Heaven. How could they be merely instruction given in reply to Fan Chi’s questions?
Nevertheless, without Zixia’s observation, “How rich in meaning!”, Confucius’s teaching concerning the crooked and the upright would have remained obscure forever. A man of earlier times said: “To unfold the sage’s hidden meanings and teach…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
萬世無窮者顏子也斯於子夏亦云
唯天下至聖爲能聰明睿知足以有臨也
邢鳳毛
同考試官教諭謝　批〔聰明睿知一節發用即非等閒此作〕
考試官教諭張　批〔專主燕甚在心且下句以有臨取足於聰明睿知非造理精密者孰能作此宜高薦〕
考試官學正高　批〔體認精到發揮明徹〕
〔學業純正足冠多士〕
聖人質超乎天下而君道豫焉蓋居上克明君
道也聖人獨稟乎生知之質有不足以居上而
臨下也哉中庸明天道意謂天地聖人相爲一
===
體者也觀天道之小德者亦觀之聖人而已矣
何則聖人者同賦于天而爲天之獨厚者也同
具于人而爲人之特出者也故自其質而言之
清淑之畀于太和者既獨鍾夫純粹之正虛靈
之凝于保合者又克全其明覺之常內境昭融
而不睹不聞之中聰明具焉一天道之清通而
無所蔽也神靈天啓而無思無爲之地睿知存
焉一日月之貞明而不可眩也夫然則萃繼
punctuated:
萬世無窮者，顏子也。斯於子夏亦云。

唯天下至聖，爲能聰明睿知，足以有臨也。

邢鳳毛

同考試官教諭謝，批〔聰明睿知一節，發用即非等閒，此作〕。
考試官教諭張，批〔專主燕甚在心，且下句以有臨取足於聰明睿知，非造理精密者，孰能作此？宜高薦〕。
考試官學正高，批〔體認精到，發揮明徹〕〔學業純正，足冠多士〕。

聖人質超乎天下，而君道豫焉。蓋居上克明，君道也。聖人獨稟乎生知之質，有不足以居上而臨下也哉？中庸明天道，意謂天地聖人相爲一體者也。觀天道之小德者，亦觀之聖人而已矣。何則？聖人者，同賦于天，而爲天之獨厚者也；同具于人，而爲人之特出者也。故自其質而言之，清淑之畀于太和者，既獨鍾夫純粹之正；虛靈之凝于保合者，又克全其明覺之常。內境昭融，而不睹不聞之中，聰明具焉，一天道之清通而無所蔽也；神靈天啓，而無思無爲之地，睿知存焉，一日月之貞明而不可眩也。夫然，則萃繼
translation_en:
…for ten thousand generations without end: this was Master Yan. The same may also be said of Zixia.

“Only the utmost sage under Heaven possesses the keenness of hearing, clarity of sight, sagacity, and wisdom sufficient to preside over others.”

Xing Fengmao

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor: 〔In this composition, the exposition of the passage on keenness of hearing, clarity of sight, sagacity, and wisdom is already extraordinary in its treatment of their operation.〕
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔It concentrates specifically on ‘yan shen’ within the mind [?]. Moreover, it takes the following phrase, ‘sufficient to preside over others,’ as finding its sufficiency in keenness of hearing, clarity of sight, sagacity, and wisdom. Who could write this without a precise and thorough grasp of principle? It merits recommendation at a high rank.〕
Comment by Examiner Gao, Director of Studies: 〔Its understanding is exact and penetrating; its exposition lucid and thorough.〕〔His learning is pure and correct, sufficient to place him foremost among the many candidates.〕

The sage’s innate endowment surpasses that of all under Heaven, and the Way of the ruler is already implicit in it. For to occupy a superior position and be capable of clear discernment is the Way of the ruler. The sage alone receives the innate endowment of one who knows from birth. Could he possibly lack what is needed to occupy a superior position and preside over those below? In elucidating the Way of Heaven, the Doctrine of the Mean means that Heaven, Earth, and the sage together form a single body. To observe the lesser powers of the Way of Heaven, one need only observe the sage.

Why is this? The sage shares with others an endowment from Heaven, yet Heaven has been exceptionally generous to him. He possesses what other human beings possess, yet stands out uniquely among them. Thus, speaking of his innate endowment, the clarity and goodness bestowed upon him by the Supreme Harmony concentrate uniquely in him the rectitude of unalloyed purity. The numinous receptivity consolidated through the preservation of harmony also fully retains the constancy of his luminous awareness. His inner realm is radiant and unobstructed; amid what is neither seen nor heard, keenness of hearing and clarity of sight are fully present. These are one with the clarity and free passage of Heaven’s Way, without anything to obscure them. His spiritual intelligence is opened by Heaven; in the realm of neither thought nor action, sagacity and wisdom abide. These are one with the constant brightness of the sun and moon, incapable of being confounded. This being so, he gathers together and carries forward…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
于天地之間其爲氣也配義與道無是
餒也是集義所生者非義襲而取之也
行有不慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未
甞知義以其外之也必有事焉而勿正
心勿忘勿助長也
高士徵
同考試官教諭孟　批〔辭間理足且莊嚴中有順題錯〕
〔綜者在心思筆力俱到宜錄以式〕
考試官教諭張　批〔渾融充使是養浩然有得者〕
考試官學正高　批〔善發孟子之蘊〕
===
大賢詳論浩然之氣惟在所養而已矣甚矣氣
本浩然也善養之則塞天地而配道義矣集義
養氣之功寧容已哉孟子告公孫丑之意若曰
浩然之氣固難言矣然豈終無可言耶吾甞反
而觀之但見其爲氣也至大而不可禦焉至剛
而無所撓焉蓋天地與我之正氣也人患無以
養之耳苟能直養而無以害之則氣之剛大者
適得吾體自與天地相似而充塞之無間矣豈
punctuated:
于天地之間。其爲氣也，配義與道；無是，餒也。是集義所生者，非義襲而取之也。行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰告子未甞知義，以其外之也。必有事焉而勿正，心勿忘，勿助長也。

高士徵

同考試官教諭孟，批〔辭間理足，且莊嚴中有順題錯〕〔綜者在，心思筆力俱到，宜錄以式。〕
考試官教諭張，批〔渾融充使，是養浩然有得者。〕
考試官學正高，批〔善發孟子之蘊。〕

大賢詳論浩然之氣，惟在所養而已矣。甚矣，氣本浩然也！善養之，則塞天地而配道義矣。集義養氣之功，寧容已哉？孟子告公孫丑之意若曰：浩然之氣固難言矣，然豈終無可言耶？吾甞反而觀之，但見其爲氣也，至大而不可禦焉，至剛而無所撓焉，蓋天地與我之正氣也。人患無以養之耳。苟能直養而無以害之，則氣之剛大者適得吾體，自與天地相似，而充塞之無間矣。豈
translation_en:
…between Heaven and Earth. As vital energy, it accords with righteousness and the Way; without these, it starves. It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds, rather than acquired by seizing upon righteousness in an isolated act. If one's conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, it starves. Thus I say that Gaozi has never understood righteousness, because he regards it as external. One must keep working at it without anticipating results; the heart must neither forget it nor help it grow by force.

Gao Shizheng

Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor, comments: 〔The wording fully conveys the principles; amid its solemn dignity there is a weaving〕〔together that follows the examination topic. Thought and literary execution are both accomplished. It should be recorded as a model.〕
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Thoroughly integrated and full [?]: this is the work of someone who has achieved something in nourishing the vast, flowing vital energy.〕
Examiner Gao, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔It skillfully brings out the deeper meaning of Mencius.〕

The great worthy's detailed discussion of the vast, flowing vital energy concerns nothing more than its nourishment. How profound it is that vital energy is inherently vast and flowing! Nourish it well, and it fills Heaven and Earth and accords with the Way and righteousness. How could the work of accumulating righteousness and nourishing vital energy ever cease? The meaning of what Mencius told Gongsun Chou was as follows: The vast, flowing vital energy is indeed difficult to describe, yet can there ultimately be nothing to say about it? I have turned inward and examined it, and have seen only that, as vital energy, it is supremely great and cannot be resisted, supremely firm and cannot be bent. It is the upright vital energy shared by Heaven, Earth, and myself. The trouble is simply that people lack the means to nourish it. If one can nourish it with uprightness and do nothing to harm it, then this firm and great vital energy finds its proper abode in my person. Of itself, it conforms to Heaven and Earth and fills them without a gap. Could it…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
特爲體之充耶氣之流行者不失吾常道義所
在自相資而互發矣苟無是氣道義豈可以虛
行耶夫氣之養成也如此然始養也何如哉蓋
必精義之功已得於積累之久是以浩然之氣
自生於養盛之餘耳固非可以襲取於外而得
之也若行一不得於心則氣自不充於體矣義
豈在外乎彼告子以義爲外者正不知所謂義
也亦安知所謂集哉是故善養氣者要必以集
義爲事而所以戒襲求慊者務事事之合宜至
===
於效之未臻也則不可先焉其或未充也尤必
以集義爲心而所以去餒思充者惟亹亹而匪
懈至於功之未致也則不可强焉夫有事勿忘
旣盡夫直養之功勿正勿助又無所謂作爲之
害如是而剛大之氣自全於我矣尚何天地之
不塞而道義之不配哉抑論性不論氣不備蓋
性者天地之原而道義之統也理氣相須所以
塞而配之者氣之能也所以集而養之者理之
宰也然則善養氣者固所以善養其性歟彼告
punctuated: 特爲體之充耶？氣之流行者，不失吾常，道義所在，自相資而互發矣。苟無是氣，道義豈可以虛行耶？夫氣之養成也如此，然始養也何如哉？蓋必精義之功已得於積累之久，是以浩然之氣自生於養盛之餘耳，固非可以襲取於外而得之也。若行一不得於心，則氣自不充於體矣。義豈在外乎？彼告子以義爲外者，正不知所謂義也，亦安知所謂集哉？是故善養氣者，要必以集義爲事，而所以戒襲求慊者，務事事之合宜。至於效之未臻也，則不可先焉。其或未充也，尤必以集義爲心，而所以去餒思充者，惟亹亹而匪懈。至於功之未致也，則不可强焉。夫有事勿忘，旣盡夫直養之功；勿正勿助，又無所謂作爲之害。如是而剛大之氣自全於我矣，尚何天地之不塞而道義之不配哉？抑論性不論氣，不備。蓋性者，天地之原而道義之統也。理氣相須，所以塞而配之者，氣之能也；所以集而養之者，理之宰也。然則善養氣者，固所以善養其性歟？彼告
translation_en:
…merely serve to fill the body? As this vital force (qi) circulates, it does not depart from my constant norm; wherever the Way and righteousness reside, they and this vital force sustain and bring forth one another. Without this vital force, how could the Way and righteousness operate in emptiness? Such is the result when the cultivation of vital force is complete. But how does its cultivation begin? Only after the work of discerning righteousness precisely has borne fruit through long accumulation does the flood-like vital force arise of itself from abundant cultivation. It certainly cannot be obtained by seizing it from outside through an isolated righteous act. If even one action fails to satisfy the heart, the vital force will of itself fail to fill the body. How could righteousness be external? Gaozi, who regarded righteousness as external, simply did not understand what righteousness means. How, then, could he understand what its accumulation means?
Thus, those skilled at cultivating vital force must make accumulating righteousness their task. To guard against grasping at righteousness through isolated acts and to seek satisfaction within, they must ensure that every undertaking accords with what is right. When the results have not yet arrived, they must not anticipate them. If their vital force is still not full, they must especially set their hearts on accumulating righteousness. To dispel its depletion and seek its fullness, they need only work diligently without slackening. When their efforts have not yet reached fruition, they must not force the outcome. By keeping to their task and never forgetting it, they fully accomplish the work of nourishing it with uprightness; by neither anticipating results nor helping its growth along, they also avoid the harm caused by contrived intervention. In this way, the firm and vast vital force becomes complete within me of itself. How, then, could it fail to fill Heaven and Earth and accord with the Way and righteousness?
Moreover, to discuss human nature without discussing vital force is incomplete. Human nature is the source of Heaven and Earth and the unifying principle of the Way and righteousness. Principle and vital force depend upon one another: filling Heaven and Earth and according with the Way and righteousness are capacities of vital force; accumulating righteousness and thereby nourishing vital force are governed by principle. Thus, is being skilled at cultivating vital force precisely the means of being skilled at cultivating one's nature? That Gao…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
會之所趨而象服之制創焉質極而示之以文
初非强人以不欲也緣羣情之所向而華躬之
章立焉儉極而導之以禮初非容心以紛更也
由是以辨上下則禮讓之風斯興舉天下鄙陋
之習而相率于雍容之美有不知誰之所爲矣
以别等威而文爲之盛斯著舉一世渾樸之俗
而相忘于熙明之天有不知帝之爲力矣我無
所爲而四方恊從欲之治風俗自是其可同矣
所謂一通變而民不倦焉非以此哉上無所作
===
而萬邦成於變之化治敎自是其休明矣所謂
一神化而民自宜焉不以是哉謂之曰垂衣裳
而天下治信乎一乾坤變化而無爲也三聖所
以繼天立極者蓋如此雖然天下有得與民變
革者制也有不得與民變革者道也三聖衣裳
之制猶之網罟耒耜而已乃其河圖之受精一
執中之旨上遡犧皇之秘下垂道統之傳夫寧
有二哉厥後非天子不制度而欲制度者其可
不求諸道乎
punctuated:
會之所趨，而象服之制創焉。質極而示之以文，初非强人以不欲也；緣羣情之所向，而華躬之章立焉。儉極而導之以禮，初非容心以紛更也。由是以辨上下，則禮讓之風斯興；舉天下鄙陋之習，而相率于雍容之美，有不知誰之所爲矣。以别等威，而文爲之盛斯著；舉一世渾樸之俗，而相忘于熙明之天，有不知帝之爲力矣。我無所爲，而四方恊從，欲之治風俗，自是其可同矣。所謂一通變而民不倦焉，非以此哉？上無所作，而萬邦成於變之化，治敎自是其休明矣。所謂一神化而民自宜焉，不以是哉？謂之曰：「垂衣裳而天下治。」信乎，一乾坤變化而無爲也。三聖所以繼天立極者，蓋如此。

雖然，天下有得與民變革者，制也；有不得與民變革者，道也。三聖衣裳之制，猶之網罟耒耜而已。乃其河圖之受，精一執中之旨，上遡犧皇之秘，下垂道統之傳，夫寧有二哉？厥後非天子不制度，而欲制度者，其可不求諸道乎？
translation_en:
…the direction in which things converged, and thus the system of emblematic robes was created. When plainness reached its extreme, they displayed refinement to the people; they never intended to force upon people what they did not desire. Following the inclinations shared by all, they established patterned insignia to adorn the person. When frugality reached its extreme, they guided people through ritual; they never harbored an intention to introduce disruptive changes. By distinguishing those above from those below, they brought forth a spirit of ritual propriety and deference. Throughout the realm, people abandoned coarse and uncultivated habits and led one another toward graceful dignity, without knowing who had brought this about. By distinguishing ranks and their proper dignities, they made the splendor of ceremonial forms manifest. An entire age’s rustic simplicity was transformed, and people lived unselfconsciously beneath a radiant and enlightened heaven, unaware that the emperor’s efforts had accomplished it. “I take no action,” yet the four quarters follow in harmony. The desired ordering of customs [?] could thereby become uniform. Is this not what is meant by bringing change into accord so that the people do not grow weary? Those above undertake no action, yet the myriad states are perfected through transforming influence; governance and instruction thereby become excellent and enlightened. Is this not what is meant by unifying through numinous transformation so that the people naturally find what suits them? It is said: “They let their upper and lower garments hang down, and the world was well governed.” Truly, this was to be at one with the transformations of Heaven and Earth and to act without deliberate striving. Such, indeed, was how the Three Sages continued Heaven’s work and established the supreme standard.

Nevertheless, in the world there are things that may be changed together with the people: institutions. There is something that may not be changed together with the people: the Way. The Three Sages’ system of upper and lower garments was simply like the invention of nets and plowing implements. But as for receiving the River Chart and the purport of being refined and single-minded and holding fast to the Mean—tracing these upward to the mysteries of Fuxi and transmitting downward the succession of the Way—could these ever have been two different things? Thereafter, none but the Son of Heaven was entitled to establish institutions and standards. Could anyone wishing to establish them fail to seek their basis in the Way?

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
業業焉求以克勝之也君臣克艱如此吾見脩
政之功足以振精明之治而綱舉目張上無不
乂之政矣化民之術足以速觀感之機而遷善
協中下皆敏德之民矣豈非效之必至者哉然
大禹祗承之心即帝舜保治之心也於是帝聞
其言而俞之曰德業成於上下之交事功起於
明良之會信能克艱其效豈但已哉將見延納
既廣而嘉謨起樂告之誠善無不言言無不盡
也寧有隱伏者耶明揚有道而黎獻遂登庸之
===
願知無不舉舉無不先也奚有遺佚者耶道化
孚而兆民得所膏澤究而天下舉安萬邦奚有
弗寧者耶蓋至是而政乂民化之效益廣矣豈
非君臣克艱之所致哉是則大禹之謨責難之
敬也帝舜之言樂取之誠也虞廷都俞之盛如
此此其治之不可及歟抑舜禹君臣艱罔弗克
治罔弗隆而其相戒之辭恒惴惴若不及者是
豈作而致其情哉其心誠以天下至廣萬民至
衆有一不得其所皆予責也故曰危微曰儆戒
punctuated: 業業焉求以克勝之也。君臣克艱如此，吾見脩政之功足以振精明之治，而綱舉目張，上無不乂之政矣；化民之術足以速觀感之機，而遷善協中，下皆敏德之民矣。豈非效之必至者哉？然大禹祗承之心，即帝舜保治之心也。於是帝聞其言而俞之曰：「德業成於上下之交，事功起於明良之會。信能克艱，其效豈但已哉？將見延納既廣，而嘉謨起樂告之誠，善無不言，言無不盡也，寧有隱伏者耶？明揚有道，而黎獻遂登庸之願，知無不舉，舉無不先也，奚有遺佚者耶？道化孚而兆民得所，膏澤究而天下舉安，萬邦奚有弗寧者耶？」蓋至是而政乂民化之效益廣矣，豈非君臣克艱之所致哉？是則大禹之謨，責難之敬也；帝舜之言，樂取之誠也。虞廷都俞之盛如此，此其治之不可及歟？抑舜禹君臣，艱罔弗克，治罔弗隆，而其相戒之辭恒惴惴若不及者，是豈作而致其情哉？其心誠以天下至廣，萬民至衆，有一不得其所，皆予責也。故曰危微，曰儆戒，
translation_en:
…with anxious vigilance, seeking to overcome it. When ruler and minister thus undertake what is difficult, I see that their efforts to improve government will suffice to invigorate enlightened rule: once the main cord is raised, every mesh of the net opens, and above, no affair of government will remain disordered. Their means of transforming the people will suffice to hasten the people's response to the example they behold: turning toward goodness and conforming to the mean, those below will all become people diligent in virtue. Are these not results that must necessarily follow?

Yet the heart with which the Great Yu reverently received his charge was precisely the heart with which Emperor Shun preserved good government. Thus, hearing his words, the emperor assented, saying: “Virtuous achievement is accomplished through interaction between those above and those below; successful undertakings arise from the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers. If they truly can undertake what is difficult, how could the effects stop at this? We shall see that, as the reception of counsel becomes extensive, excellent plans arise from a sincere delight in offering advice. No good proposal goes unspoken, and nothing spoken is left incompletely expressed. Could anything remain concealed? When the worthy are discerningly brought forward by proper means, the worthies among the people fulfill their wish to enter service. None who are known go unrecommended, and none recommended fail to receive precedence. How could any worthy remain overlooked? When the transforming influence of the Way wins trust, the myriad people find their proper place; when beneficence reaches everywhere, all under Heaven enjoy peace. How could any of the myriad states remain unsettled?”

At this point, the effects of orderly government and the people's transformation become still more extensive. Is this not brought about by ruler and minister undertaking what is difficult? Thus, the Great Yu's counsels express the reverence of holding one's ruler to difficult tasks; Emperor Shun's words express a sincere delight in accepting good counsel. Such was the flourishing exchange of praise and assent at the court of Yu! Is this why its government could not be equaled?

Moreover, as ruler and minister, Shun and Yu left no difficulty unmastered and brought government to the height of flourishing. Yet in their words of mutual admonition they were always apprehensive, as though falling short. Could this have been a feeling they affected and artificially produced? In their hearts they truly thought: “The realm is exceedingly vast, and its people exceedingly numerous. If even one person fails to find a proper place, the responsibility is mine.” Thus they spoke of peril and subtlety, and of vigilance and admonition…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
曰兢業其言不同其旨則一矣故曰聖人之心
無窮又曰聖人不以吾治爲已足有以哉
穆穆在上明明在下灼于四方　張允升
同考試官教諭謝　批〔虞廷君臣去此時遠矣呂刑〕〔蓋追叙之詞也作形容穆穆明明宛乎目前且文詞典則非〕
凡格此取之
考試官教諭張　批〔不藁時套雅有矩度〕
考試官學正高　批〔精切不浮〕
===
聖世君臣德容之盛而達於無間者也蓋穆穆
明明德之著於容者盛矣而光輝四達焉自非
虞世君臣能如是乎宜穆王申言以訓刑也蓋
謂聖人之御世也不徒任法以維治而惟尚德
以化民吾嘗上嘉有虞而想見其盛矣是故穆
穆者和敬之容也惟帝舜之爲君也而德威德
明焉則純粹之懿著之爲雍肅之儀大和洋溢
藹乎其可親也至敬流通儼乎其可象也在上
何穆穆乎明明者精白之容也今三后之爲臣
punctuated:
曰兢業，其言不同，其旨則一矣。故曰：「聖人之心無窮。」又曰：「聖人不以吾治爲已足。」有以哉！

穆穆在上，明明在下，灼于四方。　張允升

同考試官教諭謝　批〔虞廷君臣去此時遠矣，《呂刑》〕〔蓋追叙之詞也。作形容穆穆、明明，宛乎目前，且文詞典則，非〕凡格，此取之。

考試官教諭張　批〔不藁時套，雅有矩度。〕

考試官學正高　批〔精切不浮。〕

聖世君臣德容之盛，而達於無間者也。蓋穆穆、明明，德之著於容者盛矣，而光輝四達焉，自非虞世君臣，能如是乎？宜穆王申言以訓刑也。蓋謂聖人之御世也，不徒任法以維治，而惟尚德以化民。吾嘗上嘉有虞，而想見其盛矣。是故穆穆者，和敬之容也。惟帝舜之爲君也，而德威德明焉，則純粹之懿著之爲雍肅之儀，大和洋溢，藹乎其可親也；至敬流通，儼乎其可象也。在上何穆穆乎！明明者，精白之容也。今三后之爲臣
translation_en:
…They speak of being vigilant and diligent: their words differ, but their purport is one. Thus it is said, “The sage’s concern knows no bounds,” and again, “The sage does not regard his own good government as sufficient.” There is good reason for these sayings!

“Reverently harmonious above, brilliantly discerning below, shining throughout the four quarters.” — Zhang Yunsheng

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor: “The rulers and ministers of the court of Yu were already far removed from that time. ‘The Punishments of Lü’ is therefore a retrospective account. This composition portrays their reverent harmony and brilliant discernment as though they were before our eyes. Moreover, its language is classical and well regulated, beyond the ordinary standard. For this reason it is selected.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “It avoids the conventional formulas of the day [?] and displays refined compositional discipline.”

Comment by Examiner Gao, School Instructor: “Precise and incisive, without superficiality.”

Such was the splendor of the virtue manifested in the bearing of ruler and ministers in a sagely age, reaching everywhere without obstruction. Reverent harmony and brilliant discernment: virtue manifested in their bearing was abundant, and its radiance spread in all directions. Who but the ruler and ministers of the age of Yu could have achieved this? Fittingly, King Mu reiterated these words in his instructions concerning punishments. His meaning was that, in governing the world, a sage does not merely rely upon laws to maintain order, but esteems virtue to transform the people. “I have long looked back with admiration upon the age of Yu and pictured its grandeur.”

Thus, reverent harmony is a bearing of concord and respect. As ruler, Emperor Shun inspired awe through virtue and displayed illumination through virtue. His pure excellence manifested itself in a dignified and solemn demeanor. Supreme harmony overflowed, making him gracious and approachable; utmost reverence pervaded him, making him august and worthy of emulation. How reverently harmonious he was above! Brilliant discernment is a bearing of unalloyed purity. Now, as for the three lords serving as ministers…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
也而恤功于民焉則憂勤之心彰之爲昭融之
象勵精煥發而熙載者日宣也明作奮揚而亮
工者日嚴也在下何明明乎君臣之德徵諸容
者如此由是有道之氣象自宣夫赫奕之休而
合四方以勤施初不見其或禦令德之威儀自
著夫輝煌之盛而盡四表以光被殆不見其或
遺和敬形于一人而英華達於四訖自邇以及
遠旁燭其無疆焉浩浩乎徧及之神何者不在
其文明之中乎精白凝於羣后而光輝至於四
===
敷由中以達外於昭其無間焉蕩蕩乎廣運之
妙何者不在其照臨之下乎吁此君臣昭德以
化民殆有出於法制之外而不徒恃乎刑者矣
典獄者其尚鑒之抑帝王之治法天者也天之
道先陽而後陰故聖之治先德而後刑而協中
之化萬古稱隆焉後世任法律而不知有仁義
者不罪於帝王寧不媿於呂刑乎此呂刑之所
以見錄於書也
詩
punctuated:
也，而恤功于民焉，則憂勤之心彰之爲昭融之象。勵精煥發，而熙載者日宣也；明作奮揚，而亮工者日嚴也。在下何明明乎！君臣之德徵諸容者如此，由是有道之氣象，自宣夫赫奕之休，而合四方以勤施，初不見其或禦；令德之威儀，自著夫輝煌之盛，而盡四表以光被，殆不見其或遺。和敬形于一人，而英華達於四訖，自邇以及遠，旁燭其無疆焉。浩浩乎徧及之神，何者不在其文明之中乎！精白凝於羣后，而光輝至於四敷，由中以達外，於昭其無間焉。蕩蕩乎廣運之妙，何者不在其照臨之下乎！吁！此君臣昭德以化民，殆有出於法制之外，而不徒恃乎刑者矣。典獄者其尚鑒之！抑帝王之治，法天者也。天之道先陽而後陰，故聖之治先德而後刑，而協中之化，萬古稱隆焉。後世任法律而不知有仁義者，不罪於帝王，寧不媿於呂刑乎？此呂刑之所以見錄於書也。

詩
translation_en:
…as ministers, they attend diligently to their work for the people; thus their anxious, industrious hearts manifest themselves in an appearance of luminous harmony. Their concentrated energies shine forth, and their advancement of affairs becomes daily more evident; they act with discernment and exert themselves, and their fulfillment of their duties becomes daily more exacting. How radiant are those below! Such is the virtue of ruler and ministers as manifested in their bearing. From this, the presence of a government possessing the Way naturally displays its splendid beauty: it embraces all four quarters in its diligent beneficence, encountering no apparent resistance. The dignified bearing of excellent virtue naturally reveals its brilliant magnificence: its light covers the utmost bounds of the world, seemingly leaving nothing out. Harmony and reverence take visible form in the One Man, and their flowering excellence reaches the four limits. From near to far, they cast their light in every direction without bounds. Vast indeed is this all-pervading spiritual efficacy! What does not lie within its civilizing radiance? Purity gathers in the assembled ministers, and their brilliance spreads in all four directions. From within it reaches outward, shining without interruption. Boundless indeed is the wondrous reach of its influence! What does not lie beneath its illumination?

Ah! By making their virtue manifest to transform the people, this ruler and his ministers surely achieved something beyond laws and institutions, without relying solely upon punishments. Let those responsible for judicial proceedings take this as their mirror! Moreover, the government of emperors and kings models itself upon Heaven. The Way of Heaven puts yang before yin; hence the government of sages puts virtue before punishment. Its transforming influence, harmonizing with the mean, has been acclaimed through all ages as supreme. Those of later ages who rely on laws and know nothing of benevolence and righteousness—even if they are not condemned by the emperors and kings, can they fail to feel shame before “The Punishments of Lü”? This is why “The Punishments of Lü” was included in the Book of Documents.

Book of Odes

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
中正鳲鳩在桑其子在棘淑人君子其儀不忒
其儀不忒正是四國
侯于曾
同考試官教諭李　批〔不忒正四國處塲中類多浮泛可厭此作真切精當善形容風人之意是宜錄出〕
考試官教諭張　批〔體裁嚴整詞氣明亮正身率物之意儼然溢目蓋潛心於經學者〕
考試官學正高　批〔莊重溫雅〕
===
詩人美君子而興其身之爲度焉蓋威儀者身
之章也君子有不忒之儀則可以爲度矣謂不
足以正四國哉鳲鳩之詩美君子用心之善也
想其託興之意若曰心者萬化之原而身者四
方之極也吾茲有感於君子矣彼鳲鳩在桑其
子在棘焉是不以子而易其所止之常也在物
固有然者矣況我淑人君子耶本之以如結之
心既立夫方外之體形而爲有常之度自協乎
中正之觀施於四體不惟其儀之一也致禮以
punctuated:
中正。鳲鳩在桑，其子在棘。淑人君子，其儀不忒。其儀不忒，正是四國。
侯于曾。
同考試官教諭李批〔不忒正四國處，塲中類多浮泛可厭。此作真切精當，善形容風人之意，是宜錄出。〕

Centrality and correctness.
“The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree; its young are in the thorn trees. The good man, the gentleman—his deportment does not err. His deportment does not err, and he thereby sets right the states in all four quarters.”
Hou Yuzeng.
Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔On the passage about unerring deportment setting right the states in all four quarters, examination essays are mostly superficial and vague, to a tiresome degree. This composition is concrete, sincere, precise, and apt. It ably conveys the intention of the poet of the Airs and deserves to be selected for inclusion.〕
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Its structure is rigorous and orderly, its language and tenor clear and bright. The idea of rectifying oneself to lead others stands vividly before the eyes. Its author must be someone who has devoted himself deeply to studying the Classics.〕
Examiner Gao, Instructor, comments: 〔Dignified, measured, and refined.〕
The poet praises the gentleman and uses an evocative image to show how his person serves as a standard. For dignified deportment is the outward manifestation of the person. If the gentleman’s deportment is unerring, he can serve as a standard. Could one say that he is insufficient to set right the states in all four quarters? The poem “The Cuckoo” praises the goodness with which the gentleman applies his mind. We may imagine the intention conveyed through its evocative image as saying: The mind is the source of all transformations, while the person is the standard for the four quarters. Here I am moved to reflect upon the gentleman. That cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, while its young are in the thorn trees: it does not change its customary resting place on account of its young. Such constancy certainly exists among other creatures; how much more, then, in our good man, the gentleman? Grounding himself in a mind as firmly bound as a knot, he has established the substance of outward rectitude. Manifested as a constant standard of conduct, this naturally accords with an appearance of centrality and correctness. title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
業者自足以成夫保障之功殫忠貞以自效所
以弘其贊相之能者自足以建夫屛翰之績自
其德之所培植也扶國運而繫人心有以鞏皇
圖于有永我周植本之固孰非其夾輔之力哉
自其才之所樹立也保人民而安社稷有以奠
國祚于無疆我周邠郿之鼎孰非其底定之勳
哉夫以王國克生乎多士固足以見天厚有周
之意多士能忠乎國家又可以見多士承天之
心則其傳世之顯也宜哉雖然周士之生固本
===
于天而文王菁莪棫樸之化所以涵濡之者久
矣其始也純德以作人其終也任賢以佐命此
文德之所以盛而天命所由歸也周公欲成王
法祖以用賢而拳拳于周士傳世之顯及召公
卷阿之詠又以得賢自輔終之老成之告君類
若此厥后成王爲有周令主者周召之功偉矣
春秋
春王正月公會齊侯宋公陳侯衞侯鄭伯
許男曹伯侵蔡蔡潰遂伐楚次于陘
punctuated:
業者，自足以成夫保障之功；殫忠貞以自效，所以弘其贊相之能者，自足以建夫屛翰之績。自其德之所培植也，扶國運而繫人心，有以鞏皇圖于有永。我周植本之固，孰非其夾輔之力哉？自其才之所樹立也，保人民而安社稷，有以奠國祚于無疆。我周邠郿之鼎，孰非其底定之勳哉？夫以王國克生乎多士，固足以見天厚有周之意；多士能忠乎國家，又可以見多士承天之心，則其傳世之顯也宜哉！雖然，周士之生固本于天，而文王菁莪棫樸之化，所以涵濡之者久矣。其始也，純德以作人；其終也，任賢以佐命。此文德之所以盛，而天命所由歸也。周公欲成王法祖以用賢，而拳拳于周士傳世之顯；及召公卷阿之詠，又以得賢自輔終之。老成之告君類若此。厥后成王爲有周令主者，周召之功偉矣！

春秋

春，王正月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衞侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯侵蔡。蔡潰，遂伐楚，次于陘。
translation_en:
…such undertakings are themselves sufficient to accomplish the work of protection. By exhausting their loyalty and steadfastness in service, they enlarge their capacity to assist their ruler and are themselves sufficient to achieve distinction as the state's bulwarks. Through what their virtue nurtures, they sustain the fortunes of the state and bind the people's hearts to it, thereby securing the imperial enterprise for all time. How could the firmly planted foundations of our Zhou be anything other than the fruit of their supporting efforts? Through what their talents establish, they protect the people and secure the altars of soil and grain, thereby ensuring the dynasty's boundless continuance. How could the tripod of our Zhou at Bin and Mei [?] be anything other than the achievement of their work of pacification?

That the royal state could produce so many worthy men certainly reveals Heaven's intention to favor Zhou. That these worthy men could be loyal to the state also reveals their resolve to uphold Heaven's will. It was therefore fitting that they should remain illustrious through successive generations! Nevertheless, although the birth of Zhou's worthy men ultimately depended upon Heaven, King Wen's transforming influence, evoked in “Luxuriant Southernwood” (Jing E) and “The Oak and the Shrub” (Yu Pu), had long nurtured them. At the outset, he cultivated men through pure virtue; in the end, he entrusted the worthy with assisting the heavenly mandate. This explains the flourishing of his civil virtue and why Heaven's mandate came to him.

The Duke of Zhou wished King Cheng to emulate his ancestor in employing the worthy, and therefore dwelt earnestly upon the enduring eminence of Zhou's men through the generations. The Duke of Shao's poem “Winding Hills” (Juan A) likewise concluded with obtaining worthy men to assist the ruler. Such was the counsel that mature and experienced statesmen gave their sovereign. That King Cheng subsequently became an excellent ruler of Zhou owed much to the great achievements of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao!

Spring and Autumn Annals

In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. …

text:

年冬公會晉侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾
子滕子薛伯杞伯小邾子齊世子光伐
鄭十有二月己亥同盟于戲〔襄公九年〕

桓之服楚悼之敵楚皆不戰而屈人兵者也其

八國之衆所爲集於陘也維時奇兵掠境而蔡

Associate Examiner Meng, Instructor, comments: 〔Most writers in the examination compound merely plagiarize arguments. In treating the intentions and actions of Dukes Huan and Dao in bringing Chu to submission, this composition is upright in principle and rigorous in expression. Following the capture of the Earl of Dan and Kong Shu’s exhortation to cultivate virtue, the forces of eight states assembled at Xing. title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
律亟退舍以結盟而下之有禮雖不必戰勝攻
取而徼好承願楚已帖然服矣不謂之善勝可
乎春秋取其近王事也是故美召陵焉畏謀不
從騑任其咎三駕之役所爲講於戲也維時鄭
待二境以請盟楚肆北圖而力競晉之伯業亦
落落乎其難合矣使忿疾者處此將不勝其求
逞之心荆尸兩廣之雄安能保其必捷乎所幸
善陣之法武子能明而悼也聽之分軍逆來而
於我未病還師許盟而彼不能從雖不必暴骨
===
以爭而大勞未艾楚已索然屈矣不謂之善勝
可乎春秋取其能駕外也是故下書蕭魚以美
焉凡此皆慎用兵重民命而惡以兵刃相接聖
人之情見已惜乎召陵之後濤塗執陳見侵桓
志已盈蕭魚之續偉矣㬥啓通吳政委大夫事
日非焉不然以桓公正而不譎晉悼君子之資
幾何而不進於王德哉此管仲知罃所以終於
伯佐而已噫覸文匿武之訓顧取威定霸者所
能乆假耶
punctuated:
律，亟退舍以結盟，而下之有禮。雖不必戰勝攻取，而徼好承願，楚已帖然服矣。不謂之善勝可乎？《春秋》取其近王事也，是故美召陵焉。
畏謀不從，騑任其咎。三駕之役，所爲講於戲也。維時鄭待二境以請盟，楚肆北圖而力競，晉之伯業亦落落乎其難合矣。使忿疾者處此，將不勝其求逞之心，荆尸兩廣之雄，安能保其必捷乎？所幸善陣之法，武子能明，而悼也聽之，分軍逆來而於我未病，還師許盟而彼不能從。雖不必暴骨以爭，而大勞未艾，楚已索然屈矣。不謂之善勝可乎？《春秋》取其能駕外也，是故下書蕭魚以美焉。
凡此皆慎用兵、重民命，而惡以兵刃相接，聖人之情見已。惜乎召陵之後，濤塗執，陳見侵，桓志已盈；蕭魚之續，偉矣㬥啓，通吳，政委大夫，事日非焉。不然，以桓公正而不譎、晉悼君子之資，幾何而不進於王德哉？此管仲、知罃所以終於伯佐而已。噫！覸文匿武之訓，顧取威定霸者所能乆假耶？
translation_en:
…with discipline; he promptly withdrew his encampment to conclude a covenant, showing courtesy in humbling himself before the other side. Without necessarily winning battles or taking territory, he sought friendly relations and accommodated their wishes, and Chu had already submitted peaceably. Could this fail to be called skill in achieving victory? The Spring and Autumn Annals approved his coming close to the achievements of a true king, and therefore praised the covenant at Shaoling.
The counsel prompted by fear was not followed, and Fei bore the blame. The campaign of three successive mobilizations arose from the negotiations at Xi. At that time, Zheng waited upon developments on its two frontiers before requesting a covenant [?], while Chu pursued its designs upon the north and competed vigorously. Jin’s enterprise of hegemony likewise seemed remote from achieving unity. Had an angry and impetuous ruler faced this situation, he could hardly have restrained his desire to prevail. Against the might of Chu’s battle formations and its two Guang chariot divisions, how could he have assured himself of victory? Fortunately, Wuzi understood the methods of effective military deployment, and Duke Dao listened to him. They divided their forces to meet the approaching enemy, without exhausting their own side; they withdrew their troops and consented to a covenant, while the other side could not keep pace. Without necessarily leaving bones exposed in armed contention, they subjected Chu to great and unremitting exertion, until it was dispirited and subdued. Could this fail to be called skill in achieving victory? The Spring and Autumn Annals approved his ability to control the external powers, and therefore subsequently recorded Xiaoyu to praise him.
All these instances show caution in employing troops, regard for the people’s lives, and aversion to the clash of weapons. The sage’s sentiments are manifest here. Alas, after Shaoling, Taotu was arrested and Chen suffered invasion: Duke Huan’s ambitions had already grown excessive. Following Xiaoyu, “grand indeed, violence opened” [?]; relations were established with Wu, government was entrusted to the grandees, and affairs deteriorated daily. Otherwise, given Duke Huan’s uprightness without deceit and Duke Dao of Jin’s qualities as a gentleman, how could they have been far from advancing to kingly virtue? This is why Guan Zhong and Zhi Ying ultimately remained merely assistants to hegemons. Alas! Could those who sought commanding power and an established hegemony long have sustained even a borrowed adherence to the injunction to manifest civil virtue and conceal military might [?]?

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
春秋四夷雖大皆曰子不以是夫然晉雖居前
吳實並霸先吳不免於拂經列書尤嫌於泯實
特書曰及而天地之大經以順會盟之霸迹足
徵使吳不得自遂其强晉不至終底於弱聖人
立法垂訓之嚴如此夫然後防立而中國有常
勝焉名正而四夷有定守焉要無事乎持衡爭
長大經一順而抑鋒止鋭亦自有餘策矣後世
乃有顛倒冠屨以有天下者將欲保國而免其
侵暴得乎噫由不講於治內御外之道故耳撥
亂世反之正非聖人其孰能之雖然聖人之不
===
得已也使中國猶有人焉蕞爾夷吳猶不能拒
於越之入何至主盟上國哉乃曾廿百牢之徵
衛懼國狗之瘈非獨晉俛首東向而聽命也若
夫持節旄以尊漢爭獻納以伸宋者其亦聞黃
池之訓而興起者與
禮記
天子者與天地參故德配天地兼利萬物
與日月並明明照四海而不遺微小其
punctuated:
《春秋》四夷雖大，皆曰子，不以是夫？然晉雖居前，吳實並霸。先吳，不免於拂經；列書，尤嫌於泯實。特書曰「及」，而天地之大經以順，會盟之霸迹足徵，使吳不得自遂其强，晉不至終底於弱。聖人立法垂訓之嚴如此。夫然後防立而中國有常勝焉，名正而四夷有定守焉。要無事乎持衡爭長，大經一順，而抑鋒止鋭亦自有餘策矣。後世乃有顛倒冠屨以有天下者，將欲保國而免其侵暴，得乎？噫！由不講於治內御外之道故耳。撥亂世，反之正，非聖人其孰能之？雖然，聖人之不得已也。使中國猶有人焉，蕞爾夷吳猶不能拒於越之入，何至主盟上國哉？乃曾廿百牢之徵，衛懼國狗之瘈，非獨晉俛首東向而聽命也。若夫持節旄以尊漢，爭獻納以伸宋者，其亦聞黃池之訓而興起者與？

禮記

天子者，與天地參，故德配天地，兼利萬物，與日月並明，明照四海而不遺微小。其
translation_en:
…In the Spring and Autumn Annals, rulers of the peoples of the four outer regions, however great their states, are all styled “viscount.” Is this not the reason? Yet although Jin occupied the foremost position, Wu in fact shared its hegemony. To place Wu first would inevitably violate the canonical principle; simply to list them would risk effacing the facts. The Sage therefore expressly wrote “together with”: the great constant principle of Heaven and Earth was thereby upheld, while the historical facts of hegemony at the covenant meeting remained evident. Wu was prevented from pursuing its strength unchecked, and Jin from sinking irrevocably into weakness. Such was the Sage’s strictness in establishing rules and transmitting instruction. Only then could boundaries be established so that the central states would enjoy lasting ascendancy, and designations be rectified so that the peoples of the four outer regions would have fixed limits to observe. Ultimately, there was no need to balance their power or contend for precedence. Once the great constant principle was upheld, there were ample means to check their onslaught and restrain their aggression. Yet in later ages there were those who inverted the proper positions of cap and shoes and thereby possessed All under Heaven. Could anyone then hope to preserve his state and escape their invasion and violence? Alas! This arose solely from a failure to study the way of governing within and resisting threats from without. Who but the Sage could bring order out of an age of disorder and restore it to rectitude? Even so, the Sage acted thus only because he had no alternative. Had the central states still possessed capable men, how could insignificant barbarian Wu—which could not even repel an invasion by Yuyue—have come to preside over a covenant among the states of the central realm? There was even the demand for a hundred sets of sacrificial animals [preceding wording unclear: 曾廿], and Wei feared the madness of the rabid dog of a state [?]. It was not Jin alone that bowed its head, faced east, and obeyed commands. As for those who upheld the yak-tail envoy’s staff to honor Han, or disputed the presentation of tribute to vindicate Song, were they too stirred to action by hearing the lesson of Huangchi?

雅頌之音行步則有環佩之聲升車則

===

旁燭微小而不遺德何明也夫天子道德之盛
punctuated:
在朝廷，則道仁聖禮義之序；燕處，則聽雅頌之音；行步，則有環佩之聲；升車，則有鸞和之音；居處有禮，進退有度，百官得其宜，萬事得其序。
閻應儒
同考試官教諭栗，批〔此題非常，作者不難於措詞，而難於體認。此篇有斟酌，有含蓄。於序宜以仁聖禮義爲辭，行步以環佩爲式。〕
考試官教諭張，批〔發揮眷盛處，明確可誦，而忠愛之意溢於言表，取之。〕
考試官學正高，批〔推重得體。〕
記者賛君德之極盛，必言其養之純而及其驗也。夫德侔造化，不易致也。苟非隨寓而純其所養之功，焉又何以獲其驗乎？記者之意若曰：德之未盛者，不足以同天；養之未純者，不足以昭德。惟天子得天之厚，而爲民之主也。吾見其道參天地，而兩儀之克配者，有以兼濟萬物而無外，道何大也！明並日明，而四表之光被者，有以旁燭微小而不遺，德何明也！夫天子道德之盛
translation_en:
…At court, he follows the ordered practice of benevolence, sagacity, ritual propriety, and righteousness; in his private leisure, he listens to the sounds of the Elegantiae and Hymns; as he walks, his jade pendants sound; when he mounts his carriage, its luan and he bells sound. His conduct in his dwelling accords with ritual propriety, and his advances and withdrawals observe due measure. The hundred officials each occupy their proper place, and all affairs follow their proper order.
Yan Yingru
Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “This topic is unusual. The writer’s difficulty lies not in choosing words but in grasping its meaning fully. This essay shows deliberation and restraint. In treating order and proper arrangement, it appropriately speaks of benevolence, sagacity, ritual propriety, and righteousness; in treating walking, it takes the jade pendants as the standard.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “Its exposition of abundant favor [?] is clear and worthy of recitation, while feelings of loyalty and love overflow beyond the words. Accept it.”
Examiner Gao, School Director, comments: “Its exaltation of the ruler is fittingly expressed.”
When the author of the Record of Rites praises the supreme fullness of the ruler’s virtue, he must speak of the purity of its cultivation and then proceed to its manifest effects. Virtue equal to the creative workings of Heaven and Earth is not easily attained. Unless one perfects the work of cultivation in every circumstance, how can one obtain its manifest effects? The author’s meaning seems to be this: virtue that has not reached fullness cannot equal Heaven; cultivation that has not attained purity cannot make virtue shine forth. It is the Son of Heaven who receives Heaven’s bounty and serves as lord of the people. I see that his Way forms a triad with Heaven and Earth: his capacity to match these two powers enables him to benefit all things together, excluding nothing. How great is his Way! His brightness rivals the sun’s brightness [?]: its radiance reaches the four extremities and illuminates even the smallest things on every side, overlooking nothing. How luminous is his virtue! Now, the fullness of the Son of Heaven’s Way and virtue…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
如此然豈自治之疎者所能致哉蓋無適而不
得其養者矣是故其在朝廷則仁聖迭運也禮
義時出也而所由不紊其序豈非備道於大觀
之地乎其在燕居則二雅必奏也三頌必陳也
而所聽不濫其音何嘗自肆於幽獨之地乎不
寧惟是其致樂以治心者雖行步升車不廢焉
而環佩鸞和相繼也其致禮以治躬者於居處
進退必謹焉而有禮有度不爽也如是而豈無
效之可言耶但見元首明而股肱爲之自良大
===
臣法而小臣廉也百官於是乎宜矣是宜者義
也而天子道義之效不可徵乎股肱良而庶事
爲之自康大綱舉而衆目張也萬事於是乎序
矣是序者禮也而天子道禮之效不可徵乎合
是而爲樂之和爲仁聖之用日月同明天地同
德由此其致矣天子之德一何盛哉抑考古之
帝王盛德大業未有不先於治已之功者故無
怠荒而克勤儉虞夏所以得天也制事制心敬
勝義勝商周所以受命也故古之大臣所以告
punctuated: 如此，然豈自治之疎者所能致哉？蓋無適而不得其養者矣。是故其在朝廷，則仁聖迭運也，禮義時出也，而所由不紊其序，豈非備道於大觀之地乎？其在燕居，則二雅必奏也，三頌必陳也，而所聽不濫其音，何嘗自肆於幽獨之地乎？不寧惟是，其致樂以治心者，雖行步升車不廢焉，而環佩鸞和相繼也；其致禮以治躬者，於居處進退必謹焉，而有禮有度不爽也。如是而豈無效之可言耶？但見元首明，而股肱爲之自良，大臣法而小臣廉也，百官於是乎宜矣。是宜者，義也，而天子道義之效不可徵乎？股肱良，而庶事爲之自康，大綱舉而衆目張也，萬事於是乎序矣。是序者，禮也，而天子道禮之效不可徵乎？合是而爲樂之和，爲仁聖之用，日月同明，天地同德，由此其致矣。天子之德一何盛哉！抑考古之帝王，盛德大業，未有不先於治已之功者。故無怠荒而克勤儉，虞夏所以得天也；制事制心，敬勝義勝，商周所以受命也。故古之大臣所以告
translation_en:
…is such; yet could anyone lax in governing himself attain it? Surely, wherever he goes, he receives moral nourishment. Thus, at court, benevolence and sagacity operate in turn, and ritual propriety and righteousness find expression as circumstances require. The course he follows does not disturb their proper order: is this not the full realization of the Way in a place exposed to public view? In his private quarters, the two sets of Odes—the Lesser and Greater Odes—must be performed, and the three sets of Hymns must be presented. The sounds he hears are never indiscriminate: when has he ever indulged himself in secluded solitude? Nor is this all. In bringing music to bear upon the governance of his mind, he does not dispense with it even when walking or mounting his carriage: the chimes of his jade pendants and carriage bells follow one another. In bringing ritual propriety to bear upon his conduct, he is invariably attentive in his daily life, in advancing and withdrawing; his observance of ritual and proper measure never errs. With this being so, could there be no effects to speak of?

We see that when the head is enlightened, the limbs naturally become worthy: the great ministers observe proper standards, and the lesser ministers are incorruptible. Thus the hundred officials fulfill their proper roles. This fitness is righteousness: can the efficacy of the Son of Heaven’s practice of righteousness not be verified here? When the limbs are worthy, the many affairs of government naturally prosper: the main cord of the net is raised, and all its meshes spread out. Thus the myriad affairs fall into order. This order is ritual propriety: can the efficacy of the Son of Heaven’s practice of ritual propriety not be verified here? Together these constitute the harmony of music and the operation of benevolence and sagacity. Matching the sun and moon in brightness and Heaven and Earth in virtue is attained through this. How flourishing is the virtue of the Son of Heaven!

Moreover, if we examine the emperors and kings of antiquity, none achieved flourishing virtue and great accomplishments without first undertaking the work of governing themselves. Thus, avoiding indolence and dissipation and practicing diligence and frugality were how Yu and Xia won Heaven’s favor. Regulating affairs and regulating the mind, allowing reverence and righteousness to prevail, were how Shang and Zhou received the Mandate. Therefore, the great ministers of antiquity, in admonishing…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
戒其君者一則曰天難諶斯一則曰克享天心
誠以人君繼天而爲之子其精神與天通一無
間理固如是耳匪引天以懼之也然則有志於
參天配天之治者其尚慎所以脩身養德以無
忘記禮者之言哉
先勞而後祿不亦易祿乎
侯有家
同考試官教諭栗　批〔理明詞暢深得 今臣敬事後食之〕
心録之以示式
===
考試官教諭張　批〔發明易祿字義 深得聖賢立言之意可謂善於講書矣宜錄以爲學者式 許〕
國子學正高　批
考試官學正高　批〔理致精切〕
君子敬其事而後其食此祿之所以易也蓋儒
者之心知盡其職而不謀利者也故先勞而後
獲其祿之也不亦易乎儒行載孔子告哀公之
意若曰純臣行義以達道不爲干祿之私明君
儲祿以養賢專爲勸事之報自夫下臣爲利祿
而效忠其道寖薄矣所謂儒者之易祿者果何
punctuated:
戒其君者，一則曰：「天難諶斯。」一則曰：「克享天心。」誠以人君繼天而爲之子，其精神與天通一無間，理固如是耳，匪引天以懼之也。然則有志於參天配天之治者，其尚慎所以脩身養德，以無忘記禮者之言哉！
先勞而後祿，不亦易祿乎？
侯有家
同考試官教諭栗　批〔理明詞暢，深得今臣敬事後食之〕心，録之以示式。
考試官教諭張　批〔發明易祿字義，深得聖賢立言之意，可謂善於講書矣。宜錄以爲學者式。許〕
國子學正高　批
考試官學正高　批〔理致精切〕
君子敬其事而後其食，此祿之所以易也。蓋儒者之心，知盡其職而不謀利者也。故先勞而後獲，其祿之也，不亦易乎？儒行載孔子告哀公之意，若曰：純臣行義以達道，不爲干祿之私；明君儲祿以養賢，專爲勸事之報。自夫下臣爲利祿而效忠，其道寖薄矣。所謂儒者之易祿者，果何
translation_en:
…in admonishing their rulers, some said, “Heaven is hard to trust,” while others said, “Be able to satisfy Heaven’s heart.” This was truly because the ruler succeeds Heaven and becomes its son; his spiritual essence communes with Heaven in uninterrupted unity. Such is the principle itself: they were not invoking Heaven to frighten him. Then should not those who aspire to a government that participates in and matches Heaven take care to cultivate themselves and nurture their virtue, never forgetting the words of those who recorded the rites?
“To put service first and emoluments afterward—is this not to hold emoluments lightly?”
Hou Youjia
Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the language fluent. It deeply captures the disposition of present-day ministers [?] to attend reverently to their duties and put their sustenance afterward. I record it to provide a model.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “It elucidates the meaning of ‘holding emoluments lightly’ and deeply grasps the intention behind the sages’ and worthies’ words. He may be called skilled at expounding the books. It should be recorded as a model for students. Xu [?].”
Gao, Instructor in the Directorate of Education: comment.
Examiner Gao, Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is precise and apposite.”
The gentleman attends reverently to his duties and puts his sustenance afterward: this is why he holds emoluments lightly. For the Confucian scholar’s concern is to fulfill his office, not to seek profit. Thus he first renders service and only afterward receives its rewards: does he not hold his emoluments lightly? The meaning of Confucius’s words to Duke Ai, recorded in “The Conduct of the Confucian Scholar,” is as though he said: A devoted minister practices righteousness to realize the Way, not out of a selfish desire to seek emoluments; an enlightened ruler provides emoluments to support worthy men, solely as a reward to encourage service. Once subordinate ministers render loyal service for profit and emoluments, their adherence to the Way grows steadily weaker. As for what is called the Confucian scholar’s holding emoluments lightly, what indeed…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
所見乎彼人臣效力於君者謂勞也勞吾所當
自盡人君恤臣之私者有祿也祿吾不敢自必
故儒者之事君以義之不可逃也而力有所必
竭焉惟知勞於王事而志必先之以責之不可
諉也而心有所必殫焉是雖祿有常秩而意不
及之始焉不敢憚於勞也所以奮庸熙載者必
勑其初若夫祿以養廉惟君所命而已而未始
萌夫覬覦之私繼焉不敢倦於勞也所以圖成
代終者必虔其後若夫祿以代耕惟上所賜而
已而未始起夫期必之念夫如是不亦易祿乎
蓋其正誼而不謀利則廉靜之操本無厚望之
私先事而能後食則忠懇之懷不暇自營之計
雖祿以天下當與賢者共之然事專報主而祿
不入心不惟以功詔祿之易也即使代耕之食
不給焉亦勿恤矣豈曰得之難也而祿之不易
哉雖養賢之祿不爲儒者靳之然志存立功而
利不遑計不惟以事負食之易也即使養廉之
具未周焉亦相忘矣豈曰畜之難也而祿之遂
punctuated: 所見乎？彼人臣效力於君者，謂勞也。勞，吾所當自盡；人君恤臣之私者，有祿也。祿，吾不敢自必。故儒者之事君，以義之不可逃也，而力有所必竭焉；惟知勞於王事，而志必先之，以責之不可諉也，而心有所必殫焉。是雖祿有常秩，而意不及之。始焉不敢憚於勞也，所以奮庸熙載者，必勑其初；若夫祿以養廉，惟君所命而已，而未始萌夫覬覦之私。繼焉不敢倦於勞也，所以圖成代終者，必虔其後；若夫祿以代耕，惟上所賜而已，而未始起夫期必之念。夫如是，不亦易祿乎？蓋其正誼而不謀利，則廉靜之操，本無厚望之私；先事而能後食，則忠懇之懷，不暇自營之計。雖祿以天下，當與賢者共之，然事專報主，而祿不入心，不惟以功詔祿之易也，即使代耕之食不給焉，亦勿恤矣。豈曰得之難也，而祿之不易哉？雖養賢之祿，不爲儒者靳之，然志存立功，而利不遑計，不惟以事負食之易也，即使養廉之具未周焉，亦相忘矣。豈曰畜之難也，而祿之遂
translation_en:
…what understanding does this reveal? The service a minister renders his ruler is called labor. In labor, I ought to exert myself fully. What a ruler provides out of concern for his minister’s personal needs is an emolument. An emolument I dare not claim as something assured to me. Thus, when a Confucian serves his ruler, he exhausts his strength because duty cannot be evaded. Knowing only to labor in the king’s service, he makes this his foremost concern; because responsibility cannot be shirked, he devotes his whole mind to it. Although emoluments have fixed grades, he gives them no thought.

At the outset, he dares not shrink from labor. In exerting his abilities and bringing his undertakings to fulfillment, he is necessarily diligent from the beginning. As for an emolument that sustains his integrity, he accepts only what his ruler ordains, never allowing a selfish desire to covet it to arise. Thereafter, he dares not weary of labor. In seeking to accomplish his work and carry his duties through to completion, he remains conscientious to the end. As for an emolument that substitutes for farming, he accepts only what his sovereign bestows, never entertaining the thought that it must assuredly be his. Is such a man not easy to remunerate?

Because he upholds righteousness without seeking profit, his incorruptible and tranquil disposition harbors no selfish expectations of generous rewards. Because he puts service first and can leave sustenance until afterward, his loyal and earnest heart has no leisure to devise plans for his own advantage. Although one who enjoys the revenues of the realm ought to share them with worthy men, the Confucian devotes his service solely to repaying his lord, and emoluments never enter his mind. It is not merely that he is easy to remunerate when emoluments are awarded according to merit [?]: even if the sustenance that substitutes for farming is insufficient, he does not worry. How could one say that obtaining such a man is difficult and that remunerating him is therefore not easy?

Although emoluments intended to support worthy men are not withheld from the Confucian, his aspirations lie in meritorious achievement, and he has no time to calculate his profit. It is not merely that he is easy to remunerate when his service earns him sustenance [?]: even if the provisions that sustain his integrity are incomplete, he puts them out of mind. How could one say that maintaining such a man is difficult and that remunerating him consequently…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
難哉是蓋處則爲純儒出則爲純臣者也豈與
徇私謀利之臣可同日語乎大抵持身事君無
二道而忠廉一心也故忠臣不私而家之厚者
於國必薄三代以下若晏平仲季文子者亦庶
幾約已爲國者乎然而功烈自卑公室自弱吾
不知其先務者何義也無已其惟鞠躬盡瘁而
不以餘財負主者歟先儒許其有儒者氣象良
以是哉
第貳場
===
論
爲政貴有以來天下之善
文在中
同考試官教諭栗　批〔宏博以藻彩而愈文充贍以〕〔琢裁而益粹且一結渾脫先秦語意蓋工於篇而邃於〕
思者敬服
同考試官教諭李　批〔議論發盈古雅充潤通〕〔義無餘蘊矣讀之令人三復不忍釋手手共三奏〕
之傑歟
punctuated:
難哉？是蓋處則爲純儒，出則爲純臣者也，豈與徇私謀利之臣可同日語乎？大抵持身事君無二道，而忠廉一心也。故忠臣不私，而家之厚者於國必薄。三代以下，若晏平仲、季文子者，亦庶幾約已爲國者乎？然而功烈自卑，公室自弱，吾不知其先務者何義也。無已，其惟鞠躬盡瘁而不以餘財負主者歟？先儒許其有儒者氣象，良以是哉！
第貳場
論
爲政貴有以來天下之善
文在中
同考試官教諭栗　批〔宏博以藻彩而愈文，充贍以〕〔琢裁而益粹。且一結渾脫先秦語意，蓋工於篇而邃於〕思者，敬服。
同考試官教諭李　批〔議論發盈，古雅充潤，通〕〔義無餘蘊矣。讀之令人三復，不忍釋手。手共三奏〕之傑歟？
translation_en:
…be difficult? Such a man is surely a true Confucian scholar in retirement and a true minister in office. How could he be spoken of in the same breath as ministers who pursue private interests and profit? In general, conducting oneself and serving one’s ruler are not two separate ways: loyalty and integrity spring from one heart. Thus a loyal minister does not act for private advantage, while one who lavishly provides for his own household necessarily gives little to the state. Since the Three Dynasties, men such as Yan Pingzhong and Ji Wenzi have perhaps come close to practicing personal frugality for the state’s sake. Yet their achievements remained meager, and their ruling houses grew weak. I do not understand what principle of rightness governed their choice of priorities. If one must identify such a man, would it not be he who devoted himself utterly to his duties and did not betray his lord by leaving surplus wealth? Earlier Confucian scholars acknowledged that he had the bearing of a true Confucian: surely this was why!
Second Session
Discourse
“In Governing, What Matters Is Having the Means to Attract All the Good in the Realm”
Wen Zaizhong
Comment by Associate Examiner Li 栗, Instructor: “Broad and comprehensive, it becomes still more elegant through literary embellishment; full and ample, it becomes still more refined through careful shaping. Moreover, the conclusion flows seamlessly, with the language and spirit of pre-Qin writings. Its author is accomplished in composition and profound in thought. I respectfully admire him.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Li 李, Instructor: “The argument unfolds abundantly; its style is classically elegant, rich, and polished. It comprehends the meaning, leaving no implications unexplored. Reading it makes one return to it repeatedly, unwilling to put it down. Is this an outstanding example of ‘three presentations’ [?]?”

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭張　批〔體格正大辭氣沖融可與論〕〔政矣宜錄以式〕
考試官學正高　批〔明暢可誦〕
天下之道忘其在我者常裕而矜其所長者必
隘君子不自足其所已能而以其所不能者取
諸人則天下之治成矣何則天下不可以徒治
也所以爲之綱維而整齊之者有政焉政以綱
維整齊乎天下則其務誠繁而吾以一人之智
力聽明役役焉圖之將見智力愈竭聰明愈困
===
而天下之治卒不可得而理矣故善圖治者以
爲吾旣以一身操可治之權則天下之才皆吾
之才天下之善皆吾之善吾惟延之以誠接之
以禮休休焉以廣其度則衆善畢集而天下有
餘治吾何爲敝精疲神以自用爲哉此好善所
以優于天下而朱子所以謂爲政者貴有以來
天下之善也且夫君子之爲天下國家也猶工
師之爲巨室也引繩墨運規矩操斧斤以爲欂
櫨榱桷枸欑戶牖有非一手一足之所能致者
punctuated:
考試官教諭張　批〔體格正大，辭氣沖融，可與論〕〔政矣。宜錄以式。〕
考試官學正高　批〔明暢可誦。〕
天下之道，忘其在我者常裕，而矜其所長者必隘。君子不自足其所已能，而以其所不能者取諸人，則天下之治成矣。何則？天下不可以徒治也。所以爲之綱維而整齊之者，有政焉。政以綱維整齊乎天下，則其務誠繁，而吾以一人之智力聽明，役役焉圖之，將見智力愈竭，聰明愈困，而天下之治卒不可得而理矣。故善圖治者以爲：吾旣以一身操可治之權，則天下之才皆吾之才，天下之善皆吾之善。吾惟延之以誠，接之以禮，休休焉以廣其度，則衆善畢集，而天下有餘治。吾何爲敝精疲神，以自用爲哉？此好善所以優于天下，而朱子所以謂爲政者貴有以來天下之善也。且夫君子之爲天下國家也，猶工師之爲巨室也。引繩墨，運規矩，操斧斤，以爲欂櫨榱桷枸欑戶牖，有非一手一足之所能致者
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: 〔Its form is upright and grand, its diction and tone harmonious and unforced: one may discuss〕〔government with such a writer. It should be recorded as a model.〕
Examiner Gao, School Instructor, comments: 〔Clear and fluent, worthy of recitation.〕
In the affairs of the world, those who forget their own abilities always have ample resources, whereas those who pride themselves on their strengths inevitably become restricted. The gentleman does not rest content with what he can already do, but draws upon others for what he cannot do; thus good government throughout the realm is achieved. Why is this? The realm cannot be governed without means. Government provides the framework that holds it together and brings it into order. Since government must hold together and order the whole realm, its tasks are indeed numerous. If I toil away at devising its administration with only one person's intelligence, strength, and perceptive faculties [?], my intelligence and strength will become ever more exhausted, my understanding ever more wearied, and ultimately the realm will still not be brought into order.
Thus one who plans well for good government reasons: Since I alone wield the authority by which order can be achieved, all the talents of the realm are my talents, and all the goodness of the realm is my goodness. I need only invite them with sincerity, receive them with ritual propriety, and broaden my capacity with generous tolerance. Then every kind of goodness will gather, and there will be more than sufficient resources to govern the realm. Why should I exhaust my essence and weary my spirit by relying solely on myself? This is why delighting in goodness gives one ample resources for governing the realm, and why Master Zhu said that those who govern must above all possess the means to attract the goodness of the realm.
Moreover, the gentleman's governance of the realm and its states and households is like a master builder's construction of a great mansion. He stretches the inked marking cord, applies compass and square, and wields axe and adze to make brackets and bearing blocks, rafters, curved timbers and clustered supports [?], doors and windows—things that a single pair of hands and feet cannot accomplish…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
使工師事事而自用之則天下之拙工也此猶
其小者也天以於穆尸其柄而日月以司暄雨
露以司潤風雷以司鼓霜雪以司斂五氣四序
以司推行夫然後天得以成其化使天而自爲
之暄爲之潤爲之鼓斂推行則天道亦幾乎息
矣況乎天下之大兆民之廣所以寄賴乎我者
饑寒昏墊之欲得其所顓明强弱之欲復其性
禮樂欲其明備政教欲其脩舉天地欲其位育
日月星辰欲其貞麗雨暘燠寒風欲其時若昆
===
蟲鳥獸草木欲其茂對四海八荒九夷百蠻欲
其撫御其責不旣重哉以如是之責而萃于吾
之一身將責以智慮乎智可以解紛也而一人
之智何以周天下之務將責以强乎强可以有
爲也而一人之强何以勝天下之繁將責以聞
識乎聞識可以給辨也而一人之聞識何以盡
天下之聰明故君子于此欲有以稱天下之責
則必深長思曰謂吾足智矣而視天下以愚可
乎謂吾强矣而視天下以弱可乎謂吾多聞識
punctuated: 使工師事事而自用之，則天下之拙工也。此猶其小者也。天以於穆尸其柄，而日月以司暄，雨露以司潤，風雷以司鼓，霜雪以司斂，五氣四序以司推行。夫然後天得以成其化。使天而自爲之暄，爲之潤，爲之鼓斂推行，則天道亦幾乎息矣。況乎天下之大，兆民之廣，所以寄賴乎我者：饑寒昏墊之欲得其所，顓明强弱之欲復其性，禮樂欲其明備，政教欲其脩舉，天地欲其位育，日月星辰欲其貞麗，雨暘燠寒風欲其時若，昆蟲鳥獸草木欲其茂對，四海八荒九夷百蠻欲其撫御。其責不旣重哉！以如是之責而萃于吾之一身，將責以智慮乎？智可以解紛也，而一人之智何以周天下之務？將責以强乎？强可以有爲也，而一人之强何以勝天下之繁？將責以聞識乎？聞識可以給辨也，而一人之聞識何以盡天下之聰明？故君子于此欲有以稱天下之責，則必深長思曰：「謂吾足智矣，而視天下以愚，可乎？謂吾强矣，而視天下以弱，可乎？謂吾多聞識
translation_en:
…If a master builder insisted on relying solely on himself in every task, he would be the most inept craftsman under Heaven. Yet this is still only a minor example. Heaven, in its profound solemnity, holds governing authority: the sun and moon oversee warmth; rain and dew, moisture; wind and thunder, stirring things into activity; frost and snow, their withdrawal; and the five climatic energies and four seasons, the onward course of change. Only then can Heaven accomplish its transforming work. If Heaven itself had to provide warmth and moisture, stir things into activity, draw them back, and carry their changes forward, then even the Way of Heaven would all but cease.

How much more is this true of the vast realm and its countless people! What they depend upon me for is this: that those suffering hunger, cold, darkness, and inundation should find their proper places; that the dull and intelligent, the strong and weak, should recover their inherent nature; that rites and music should be clearly established and complete; that government and moral instruction should be cultivated and put into effect; that Heaven and Earth should occupy their proper places and nurture life; that the sun, moon, and stars should keep to their proper stations; that rain, sunshine, warmth, cold, and wind should come in due season; that insects, birds, beasts, plants, and trees should flourish in harmony; and that the Four Seas, the Eight Outlying Regions, the Nine Yi, and the many Man peoples should be pacified and governed. Is this responsibility not exceedingly weighty?

With such responsibility concentrated upon my single person, shall I rely on intelligence and deliberation? Intelligence can resolve entanglements, but how can one person’s intelligence encompass all the affairs of the realm? Shall I rely on strength? Strength can accomplish things, but how can one person’s strength bear the realm’s manifold demands? Shall I rely on learning and knowledge? Learning and knowledge can furnish ready discernment, but how can one person’s learning and knowledge encompass all the perceptiveness and understanding in the realm?

Thus, if the gentleman wishes to measure up to his responsibility for the realm, he must reflect deeply and at length, saying: “I may consider myself sufficiently wise, but may I regard everyone under Heaven as foolish? I may consider myself strong, but may I regard everyone under Heaven as weak? I may consider myself widely learned and knowledgeable…”

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
矣而視天下以聾瞶可乎又必深長思曰大智
如舜而好問察多才藝如周公而三吐握天縱
多能如孔子而好敏求此三聖人者豈不自知
其能而好爲是屑屑然之不憚煩哉無亦以天
下之善無窮而一人有不足恃者乎故智不如
舜吾何爲而不好問且察才藝不如周公吾何
爲而不吐握天縱不如孔子吾何爲而不敏求
易曰山上有澤咸君子以虛受人言山澤之氣
乘虛而通也象曰觀其所感而天地萬物之情
可見矣感之義大矣哉詩曰采葑采菲無以下
體言葑菲小物也猶有足采焉况于善之大乎
故使爲政者必其自智自强自聞識而後用之
則山澤不相通也菲葑不足采也吾恐滿假之
態一彰而天下之智者强者多聞識者必將曰
彼智矣而何有于吾之智彼强矣而何有于吾
之强彼多聞識矣而何有于吾之聞識由是天
下之懷才抱德者皆將裹足不敢入境孰肯甘
心降氣以聽彼訑訑然之拒哉夫以天下之政
punctuated: 矣，而視天下以聾瞶，可乎？又必深長思曰：「大智如舜，而好問察；多才藝如周公，而三吐握；天縱多能如孔子，而好敏求。此三聖人者，豈不自知其能，而好爲是屑屑然之不憚煩哉？無亦以天下之善無窮，而一人有不足恃者乎？故智不如舜，吾何爲而不好問且察？才藝不如周公，吾何爲而不吐握？天縱不如孔子，吾何爲而不敏求？」易曰：「山上有澤，咸；君子以虛受人。」言山澤之氣乘虛而通也。象曰：「觀其所感，而天地萬物之情可見矣。」感之義大矣哉！詩曰：「采葑采菲，無以下體。」言葑菲小物也，猶有足采焉，况于善之大乎？故使爲政者必其自智、自强、自聞識而後用之，則山澤不相通也，菲葑不足采也。吾恐滿假之態一彰，而天下之智者、强者、多聞識者必將曰：「彼智矣，而何有于吾之智？彼强矣，而何有于吾之强？彼多聞識矣，而何有于吾之聞識？」由是天下之懷才抱德者，皆將裹足不敢入境，孰肯甘心降氣，以聽彼訑訑然之拒哉？夫以天下之政
translation_en:
…yet regard everyone under Heaven as deaf and blind—is that permissible? He must also reflect deeply: “Though Shun possessed great wisdom, he delighted in asking questions and examining what he heard. Though the Duke of Zhou possessed many talents and accomplishments, he repeatedly spat out his food and held his unbound hair to receive visitors. Though Confucius was endowed by Heaven with many abilities, he delighted in seeking knowledge diligently. Could these three sages have been unaware of their own abilities, and simply enjoyed such painstaking activity, never shrinking from its trouble? Was it not rather because the goodness in the world is inexhaustible, while the abilities of one person cannot suffice? Thus, since my wisdom falls short of Shun’s, why should I not delight in questioning and examining? Since my talents and accomplishments fall short of the Duke of Zhou’s, why should I not interrupt meals and hair-washing to receive worthy men? Since my natural gifts fall short of Confucius’s, why should I not seek knowledge diligently?”
The Book of Changes says: “Above the mountain there is a lake: Influence. The noble man accordingly receives others with an open mind.” This means that the vital forces of mountain and lake communicate through openness. The Commentary on the Images says: “Observe what they influence, and the true dispositions of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things can be seen.” How great is the significance of influence! The Book of Odes says: “Gather turnips, gather radishes; do not reject them because of their roots.” This means that even turnips and radishes, small things though they are, have something worth gathering. How much more is this true of the greatness of goodness!
Thus, if those who govern insist on relying on their own wisdom, strength, and learning before putting these to use, mountain and lake will fail to communicate, and radishes and turnips will be deemed unworthy of gathering. I fear that once their self-satisfied arrogance becomes apparent, the wise, the strong, and the widely learned throughout the realm will surely say: “He is wise already—what use has he for my wisdom? He is strong already—what use has he for my strength? He is widely learned already—what use has he for my learning?” Consequently, all those throughout the realm who possess talent and virtue will hold back, not daring to enter his territory. Who would willingly humble himself to endure such a conceited rebuff? Now, as for the governance of all under Heaven…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
待我而脩天下之治待我而成而吾方拒人千
千里之外以自用其所長則是瞳不以日月也
潤不以雨露也鼓不以風雷也斂不以霜雪也
推行不以五氣四序也其何以爲天道則是繩
墨不以衆任而以工師規矩斧斤不以衆任而
以工師欂櫨榱桷椳楔戸牖不以衆任而以工
師其冐以爲巨室君子知其然以爲吾有天下
國家之政吾治天下國家也吾治天下國家則
吾之善天下國家之善也天下國家之善吾之
===
善也何我非人何物非我由是體澤山之虛以
立其感法地山之謙以廣其益廓太公之量以
弘其受誠心以延之緩辭以道之和顔色以接
之皇皇焉如不及已未善吾舍焉人有善吾從
焉芻蕘可詢則不以人廢葑菲可采則不以物
遺禹聞之而拜吾益以旌焉周公三吐握吾百
焉由是戴仁負義之士近而州里遠而四海之
廣小而一才一藝大而馮翼孝德皆將裹糧載
質以遊于吾之庭如商賈之趨市行旅之歸家
punctuated:
待我而脩，天下之治待我而成，而吾方拒人千千里之外，以自用其所長，則是瞳不以日月也，潤不以雨露也，鼓不以風雷也，斂不以霜雪也，推行不以五氣四序也，其何以爲天道？則是繩墨不以衆任而以工師，規矩斧斤不以衆任而以工師，欂櫨榱桷椳楔戸牖不以衆任而以工師，其冐以爲巨室？
君子知其然，以爲吾有天下國家之政，吾治天下國家也。吾治天下國家，則吾之善，天下國家之善也；天下國家之善，吾之善也。何我非人？何物非我？由是體澤山之虛以立其感，法地山之謙以廣其益，廓太公之量以弘其受。誠心以延之，緩辭以道之，和顔色以接之，皇皇焉如不及。已未善，吾舍焉；人有善，吾從焉。芻蕘可詢，則不以人廢；葑菲可采，則不以物遺。禹聞之而拜，吾益以旌焉；周公三吐握，吾百焉。由是戴仁負義之士，近而州里，遠而四海之廣，小而一才一藝，大而馮翼孝德，皆將裹糧載質，以遊于吾之庭，如商賈之趨市，行旅之歸家。
translation_en:
…await me to be put in order, and good government throughout the world awaits me to be achieved. Yet if I keep others thousands upon thousands of li away and rely exclusively on my own strengths, this would be like giving light [?] without the sun and moon, moistening without rain and dew, stirring things without wind and thunder, drawing them in without frost and snow, and carrying the world forward without the five kinds of qi and the four seasons. How could this constitute the Way of Heaven? It would be like entrusting the marking line not to the assembled workers but to the master craftsman alone; entrusting the compass, square, axes, and adzes not to the assembled workers but to the master craftsman alone; and entrusting brackets, column capitals, rafters, door pivots, doorposts, doors, and windows not to the assembled workers but to the master craftsman alone. How could this make a great house [?]?
The gentleman understands this and reasons: I bear responsibility for governing the world, the state, and the family; I bring order to them. Since I govern the world, the state, and the family, my goodness is their goodness, and their goodness is mine. What in myself is not shared with others? What among things is not part of myself? Thus he embodies the receptivity of the lake above the mountain to establish mutual responsiveness, models himself on the humility of the mountain beneath the earth to extend his benefits, and enlarges his capacity to match that of Taigong, broadening what he can accommodate. He invites others with sincerity, guides them with gentle words, and receives them with a kindly countenance, anxiously intent as though he could never do enough. Where his own conduct is not good [?], he abandons it; where others possess goodness, he follows them. If grass cutters and wood gatherers can be consulted, he does not reject their words on account of who they are; if turnips and radishes are worth gathering, he does not overlook them on account of their lowliness. Yu bowed upon hearing good words; I shall go further in honoring them. The Duke of Zhou three times spat out his food or grasped his unbound hair to receive worthy men; I shall do so a hundred times. Thus men who uphold benevolence and righteousness, from nearby villages and neighborhoods to the farthest reaches of the Four Seas, possessing as little as a single talent or skill or as much as great supporting ability and filial virtue [?], will all wrap up provisions and bring introductory gifts to visit my court, like merchants hastening to market and travelers returning home.…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
吾不有其智而天下之智歸焉吾不有其强而
天下之强歸焉吾不有其聞識而天下之聞識
歸焉譬則昆山之玉隋和之寶明月之珠大阿
之劒鮮離之馬翠鳳之旗靈鼉之鼓夜光之壁
犀象之器所謂不産于秦而皆秦之有也夫然
後以天下才治天下事吾惟寧其功而已矣以
天下事付天下之能者吾惟觀其成而已矣我
無專智而有餘智我無專强而有餘强我無專
聞識而有餘聞識由之以禮樂則明備以刑政
===
則修明以饑寒昏墊則無不安其所以顓明强
弱則無不適其性以裁成其道輔相其宜則天
地可位萬物可育日月星辰可以順軌雨暘燠
寒風可以時若昆蟲草木鳥獸之繁可以時育
四海八荒九夷百蠻之在撫御者可化而歸其
始也以天下之責而統之爲一人之責其既也
以一人之責而分之爲衆人之責其究也至于
衆人之責舉而一人之責以塞故以此而君則
爲堯舜爲禹湯文武而君道成矣以此而相則
punctuated: 吾不有其智，而天下之智歸焉；吾不有其强，而天下之强歸焉；吾不有其聞識，而天下之聞識歸焉。譬則昆山之玉、隋和之寶、明月之珠、大阿之劒、鮮離之馬、翠鳳之旗、靈鼉之鼓、夜光之壁、犀象之器，所謂不産于秦而皆秦之有也。夫然後，以天下才治天下事，吾惟寧其功而已矣；以天下事付天下之能者，吾惟觀其成而已矣。我無專智而有餘智，我無專强而有餘强，我無專聞識而有餘聞識。由之以禮樂，則明備；以刑政，則修明；以饑寒昏墊，則無不安其所；以顓明强弱，則無不適其性。以裁成其道、輔相其宜，則天地可位，萬物可育，日月星辰可以順軌，雨暘燠寒風可以時若，昆蟲草木鳥獸之繁可以時育，四海八荒九夷百蠻之在撫御者，可化而歸。其始也，以天下之責而統之爲一人之責；其既也，以一人之責而分之爲衆人之責；其究也，至于衆人之責舉，而一人之責以塞。故以此而君，則爲堯舜、爲禹湯文武，而君道成矣；以此而相，則
translation_en: …I do not claim wisdom as my own, and the wisdom of all under Heaven comes to me; I do not claim strength as my own, and the strength of all under Heaven comes to me; I do not claim learning and discernment as my own, and the learning and discernment of all under Heaven come to me. It is like the jade of Mount Kun, the treasures of Sui and He, luminous pearls, the sword Tai’a, the horse Xianli, kingfisher-feather phoenix banners, drums of sacred alligator hide, night-shining jade discs [?], and vessels of rhinoceros horn and ivory: these are what are described as things not produced in Qin, yet all possessed by Qin. Only then can I employ the talents of all under Heaven to manage the affairs of all under Heaven, myself merely resting in their accomplishments [?]. Entrusting the affairs of all under Heaven to its capable people, I need only observe their completion. I possess no exclusive wisdom, yet have wisdom to spare; no exclusive strength, yet have strength to spare; no exclusive learning and discernment, yet have learning and discernment to spare. Applying this to rites and music makes them illustrious and complete; to punishments and government, well ordered and clear; to those suffering hunger, cold, distress, and inundation, it leaves none without a secure place; and to the dull and intelligent, strong and weak, it leaves none unable to fulfill their nature. By shaping and completing the Way of Heaven and Earth and assisting what is fitting to them, Heaven and Earth can take their proper places and the myriad things can flourish. Sun, moon, and stars can follow their proper courses; rain, sunshine, warmth, cold, and wind can arrive in season; and the profusion of insects, plants, birds, and beasts can grow at the appropriate times. Those within the Four Seas and Eight Wildernesses, the Nine Yi and the many Man peoples, who are under our care and governance can be transformed and give their allegiance. At the outset, the responsibilities of all under Heaven are brought together as the responsibility of one man. Subsequently, that one man’s responsibility is divided into the responsibilities of many. Ultimately, when the responsibilities of the many are discharged, the responsibility of the one man is thereby fulfilled. Thus, one who rules in this way becomes a Yao or Shun, a Yu, Tang, Wen, or Wu, and fulfills the Way of the ruler. One who serves as chief minister in this way, then…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
子孫不我能保雖近而黎民亦危而不安矣由
是觀之天下後世之利與不利而在乎一人好
善之實與不實爲政者其可以弗早辨哉
表
擬
三殿工成
欽定名額頒示中外廷臣
賀表〔嘉靖四十一年〕
高士徵
同考試官教諭謝　批〔士懋鼎新名崇三極〕
===
先皇弘功深意未易揄揚子能數詞章以宣盛美而祝願數言尤徵忠愛非徒藻
麗爲工已耳是用表出
考試官教諭張　批〔美辭宏詞舖張盛事于其身〕
伏味誠而心遊
廟廓者耶日且觀光尚占敷對
考試官學正高　批〔以盛美之言發忠愛之悃可以爲文矣〕
嘉靖四十一年某月某日恭遇
大工告成
punctuated:
子孫不我能保，雖近而黎民亦危而不安矣。由是觀之，天下後世之利與不利，而在乎一人好善之實與不實，爲政者其可以弗早辨哉？

表

擬三殿工成，欽定名額，頒示中外，廷臣賀表〔嘉靖四十一年〕

高士徵

同考試官教諭謝批〔士懋鼎新，名崇三極〕：先皇弘功深意，未易揄揚。子能數詞章以宣盛美，而祝願數言尤徵忠愛，非徒藻麗爲工已耳，是用表出。

考試官教諭張批〔美辭宏詞，舖張盛事于其身〕：伏味誠而心遊廟廓者耶？日且觀光，尚占敷對。

考試官學正高批〔以盛美之言發忠愛之悃，可以爲文矣〕。

嘉靖四十一年某月某日，恭遇大工告成，
translation_en:
…His descendants cannot preserve me; though close at hand, the common people too are imperiled and cannot rest secure. Viewed in this light, the benefit or harm to the world and to later generations depends upon whether one man's love of goodness is genuine. Can those who govern fail to discern this early?

Memorial

Draft congratulatory memorial from the court officials on the completion of the Three Halls, whose names were imperially determined and promulgated at court and throughout the realm. 〔Forty-first year of Jiajing [1562]〕

Gao Shizheng

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor: 〔The scholar strives for renewal [?]; the names exalt the Three Ultimates.〕 The late emperor's great achievement and profound intention are not easily celebrated adequately. You have been able, in these literary phrases [?], to proclaim this splendid accomplishment. Your few words of benediction particularly attest to loyalty and affection: your skill is not merely ornamental elegance. For this reason, this piece has been singled out.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: 〔Beautiful phrases and grand language expansively portray the magnificent event in its embodiment [?].〕 Humbly savoring sincerity, does his mind roam the ancestral temple's precincts [?]? Soon he will behold the splendor of the court; one may yet anticipate his formal responses there [?].

Comment by Examiner Gao, Instructor: 〔To express heartfelt loyalty and affection through words of splendid praise: this qualifies as accomplished writing.〕

On a certain day of a certain month in the forty-first year of Jiajing, we respectfully mark the completion of the great construction works …

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
欽名三殿曰
皇極
中極
建極左右樓曰文昭武成門曰會極歸極弘政
宣治頒示中外者伏以
宸宇煇煌弘規奠萬年鞏固
璇題昭揭奧義超千古維新制允斷于
睿謨工實創于
帝造臣民快覩朝野欣騰臣等誠懽誠忭稽首
===
頓首竊惟明堂日御垂衣正八表之瞻蒼
闕天開懸法儼一王之制爰自合宮啓攡
都俞攸存粤若斯干興歌芋寧有在慨卑
宮于禹夏緣茅茨之肇除仰考室于周宣
繇威靈之丕振蓋大聖有作非無事以疲
民而羣情所鍾自率工以興事彼黃龍白
虎徒侈美于遊觀迨飛羽披香曾何關于
政治茲蓋伏遇
皇帝陛下
punctuated:
欽名三殿曰「皇極」、「中極」、「建極」，左右樓曰「文昭」、「武成」，門曰「會極」、「歸極」、「弘政」、「宣治」，頒示中外者。伏以宸宇煇煌，弘規奠萬年鞏固；璇題昭揭，奧義超千古維新。制允斷于睿謨，工實創于帝造。臣民快覩，朝野欣騰。臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首。
竊惟明堂日御，垂衣正八表之瞻；蒼闕天開，懸法儼一王之制。爰自合宮啓攡，都俞攸存；粤若斯干興歌，芋寧有在。慨卑宮于禹夏，緣茅茨之肇除；仰考室于周宣，繇威靈之丕振。蓋大聖有作，非無事以疲民；而羣情所鍾，自率工以興事。彼黃龍白虎，徒侈美于遊觀；迨飛羽披香，曾何關于政治？茲蓋伏遇皇帝陛下
translation_en:
…the three halls were imperially named Huangji, Zhongji, and Jianji; the towers to the left and right, Wenzhao and Wucheng; and the gates, Huiji, Guiji, Hongzheng, and Xuanzhi. These names were proclaimed throughout the court and the realm. We humbly reflect: the imperial buildings shine resplendent, their grand design establishing enduring solidity for ten thousand years; the jewel-like inscriptions stand brilliantly displayed, their profound meaning surpassing antiquity in renewal. The plan was duly determined through Your Majesty’s sagacious deliberations; the work truly originated in Your Majesty’s creative undertaking. Subjects and people delight in beholding it; court and country overflow with joy. We, your servants, rejoice and exult, bowing our heads to the ground and kowtowing.
We humbly consider: daily Your Majesty presides in the Hall of Light, governing with robes hanging loosely and directing the gaze of the world’s eight quarters. The lofty palace gates open toward Heaven; the promulgated laws give solemn expression to the institutions of a sovereign. From the opening of the canopy of the Hegong palace [?], the spirit of sage counsel and assent was present; when the song Si Gan—“By the Riverbank”—arose, there was a place for spacious shelter and repose. We marvel at the humble palace of Yu of Xia, when thatched dwellings were first established [?]; we look up to the completion of the palace under King Xuan of Zhou, through which his majestic authority was greatly revived. When a great sage undertakes construction, it is surely not to weary the people without purpose; rather, where the hearts of all converge, they naturally lead the craftsmen in bringing the undertaking to fruition. Those Huanglong and Baihu palaces merely lavished splendor on pleasure excursions and sightseeing; as for Feiyu and Pixiang, what had they ever to do with good government? Now, indeed, we have humbly been fortunate to encounter Your Majesty the Emperor…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
正朝之地謂
皇極應
紫極之尊從殿以建以中期祇德以宰物傍屏
乃歸乃會協衆志以遵王文德昭而武功
成弛張之義以立弘其政以宣其治順化
之美斯彰是蓋萃
仁孝明聖之全格
天凝
命盡通變繼述之善知化窮神近以擴居重馭
輕之圖遠以為光前裕後之計臣等慚同
===
樗櫟叨厠巖廊幸就日於
堯天共仰
九重之渙汗想呼嵩於漢國遥聞四海之懽忻
匪徒載
北極而傾心惟深慶忭寔將擬南山以
獻祝曷罄揄揚伏願
昊眷益隆
聖祚彌篤闢四門之耳目
punctuated: 正朝之地謂皇極，應紫極之尊；從殿以建，以中期祇德以宰物，傍屏乃歸乃會，協衆志以遵王。文德昭而武功成，弛張之義以立；弘其政以宣其治，順化之美斯彰。是蓋萃仁孝明聖之全，格天凝命，盡通變繼述之善，知化窮神。近以擴居重馭輕之圖，遠以為光前裕後之計。臣等慚同樗櫟，叨厠巖廊，幸就日於堯天，共仰九重之渙汗；想呼嵩於漢國，遥聞四海之懽忻。匪徒載北極而傾心，惟深慶忭；寔將擬南山以獻祝，曷罄揄揚？伏願昊眷益隆，聖祚彌篤，闢四門之耳目。
translation_en:
…The place of the principal court is called Huangji, the Imperial Ultimate, corresponding to the dignity of the Purple Pole. The attendant halls are built accordingly, with centrality and reverent virtue as the aim in governing all things [?]; those beside the screens return and assemble [?], uniting their wills in allegiance to the sovereign. Civil virtue shines forth and military achievements are accomplished; the proper principles of relaxation and exertion are established. His government is extended and his rule made manifest, revealing the beauty of willing submission to his transforming influence.

This surely comes from possessing benevolence, filial devotion, discernment, and sagacity in their entirety, reaching Heaven and securing the Mandate, and fully realizing the excellence of adapting to change and carrying forward his predecessors’ work, understanding transformation and plumbing the mysteries of the spirit. For the present, it broadens the design by which the weighty center controls the lighter periphery; for the future, it provides a plan to glorify his forebears and enrich his successors.

We, your servants, are ashamed to resemble useless ailanthus and oak, yet undeservedly occupy places at court. Fortunate to approach the sun beneath the heaven of Yao, we together look up in reverence at the edict issuing from the ninefold palace, like sweat that cannot be recalled. We imagine the acclamations at Mount Song in the Han realm and hear from afar the rejoicing throughout the Four Seas. We do not merely uphold the Northern Pole with devoted hearts and profound jubilation; we would indeed offer blessings that liken your longevity to the Southern Mountain. How could we exhaust our praises? Prostrate, we wish that Heaven’s favor may ever increase, that your sacred imperial fortune may grow ever more secure, and that you may open the channels of hearing and sight at the four gates…

title: 隆慶四年陝西鄉試錄
text:
萬壽日躋乎公堂舞兩階之羽干衆星環拱于
帝座天合高地合厚日合臨月合照
丹扆斂五福之有常民用睦穀用成國用乂家
用康
謹奉
清禁綿百順于無替臣等無任欣躍屛營之至
表稱
賀以
聞
===
第叄場
策
第一問
邢鳳毛
同考試官教諭李　批〔證經典以釋〕
聖訓具見淵源之學且敷張明備而嗣守遠猷條規懇切忠愛之忱展卷
藹然取之
考試官教諭張　批〔以大本大智立意發揮精〕
邃評盡可佳
punctuated:
萬壽日躋乎公堂，舞兩階之羽干，衆星環拱于帝座。天合高，地合厚，日合臨，月合照，丹扆斂五福之有常；民用睦，穀用成，國用乂，家用康。謹奉清禁，綿百順于無替。臣等無任欣躍屛營之至，表稱賀以聞。
第叄場
策
第一問
邢鳳毛
同考試官教諭李，批〔證經典以釋〕聖訓，具見淵源之學，且敷張明備，而嗣守遠猷，條規懇切，忠愛之忱，展卷藹然，取之。
考試官教諭張，批〔以大本大智立意發揮精〕邃，評盡可佳。
translation_en:
…May wishes for ten thousand years of life rise daily in the ducal hall; may dancers wield feathers and shields between the two stairways, and the assembled stars encircle the imperial throne. May Heaven join in its loftiness, Earth in its depth, the sun in its oversight, and the moon in its illumination; may the vermilion throne gather the enduring Five Blessings. Thus may the people live in harmony, the grain ripen, the state enjoy good order, and households enjoy peace. Reverently attending the imperial precincts, may we perpetuate every favorable condition without decline. Your servants cannot contain their utmost joy and reverent trepidation. We submit this memorial of congratulations for Your Majesty’s hearing.
Third Session
